articles.title: Accent bias: AI models penalize certain speakers in interviews and tests, UW study finds
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Picture two job candidates giving the same answer to the same interview question, word for word. One has an American accent. The other has a Nigerian accent. Ask a leading AI model to score them, and the American will likely come out ahead.

That’s the gist of new research from the University of Washington, which tested how AI models from Google, OpenAI and Alibaba evaluated English spoken with five accents: American, British, Chinese, Indian and Nigerian.

Across job interviews, conference presentations and English proficiency tests, the models generally ranked American and British speakers highest, Indian speakers in the middle, and Chinese and Nigerian speakers lowest.

The penalty fell mostly on delivery. But content scores for Chinese and Nigerian speakers sometimes slipped, too, even though every speaker read the same script and the models were told to judge only the substance.

“Even though they repeatedly claimed Chinese and Nigerian speakers ‘mumbled’ or were ‘difficult to understand,’ the models were actually very good at transcribing the accented speech,” said Orevaoghene Ahia , a UW doctoral student in the Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering and co-lead author of the study.

The stakes go beyond a bad review. Companies increasingly use AI to screen recorded job interviews, and instructors are turning to oral exams as written work gets easier to fake with AI. At least one major English test used for visas and immigration, Pearson’s PTE Academic, relies on AI to score some spoken answers. It was given about 1.2 million times in 2023, according to figures cited in the paper.

The researchers didn’t test the actual products used by hiring platforms or test makers. How those systems work is usually not public, and the paper notes there are no public audits of AI-scored English tests that the authors know of. Instead, the team tested general-purpose models that companies could build on.

“We wanted to check these state-of-the-art models because these are what companies would deploy in a real-world setting,” said Yulia Tsvetkov , a UW associate professor in the Allen School and the study’s senior author.
The research was funded in part by gifts from Google and OpenAI, whose models were among those tested.

To understand the pattern, the researchers measured how acoustically different each accent was from American English. Chinese and Nigerian accents were the farthest away, and models’ scores dropped as that distance grew. Indian and British accents sat close to the American baseline.

The researchers suggest the bias may come from training data that describes accented speakers as unclear, from data sets that underrepresent some accents, or from training that reinforces ideas about how a professional should sound. English is an official language in Nigeria and the language of instruction in Indian schools, yet both accents scored below American and British ones.

The study is the latest in a run of UW research on AI bias. Earlier projects found that AI models favored resumes with white- and male-associated names , that politically slanted chatbots could shift people’s views , and that AI-written children’s stories nearly erased female animal characters .

The team presented the research Oct. 25 at the Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing in Budapest. Next, the researchers plan to study more accents, including regional variations within countries, and to look at how AI models handle audio in medical settings such as automated emergency response.

“For all of these, we hope that developers build and publish evaluations of their models that don’t focus only on average performance, but also break it down into subpopulations, dialects and so on,” Tsvetkov said. “We don’t want the average performance to be 97% accurate for the general population, but for a smaller group only 20%.”

articles.title: How a Starbucks drive-thru ‘fast pass’ could actually work
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Starbucks’ idea to use technology to recognize regulars at the drive-thru is getting plenty of attention , but the actual implementation might not be as sci-fi as some of the headlines suggest.

CEO Brian Niccol said on the company’s earnings call last week that the coffee giant is “exploring experiences that recognize participating customers as they arrive, present personalized digital menus, and make payment more effortless.”

He didn’t say how that would work, and some reports quickly jumped to the conclusion that facial recognition could be coming to Starbucks — with one headline declaring that the company wants AI to know your face .

That may be a leap. Niccol’s own description of the idea, in an interview the next morning, centered on the Starbucks app: “When you pull up to the drive-thru, if you’re in our app, it will recognize you,” he told Yahoo Finance’s Brian Sozzi . “It’ll show the order that you’ve placed historically or the last time you ordered.”
From there, he said, “the barista will be like, ‘Brian, is it the usual?’ You’ll be like, ‘Yes, great. It’s paid.’ Now you’re off to the window to pick up your drink, and out you go.”
Niccol said it will be “the fastest drive-thru experience you can have,” adding, “We haven’t named it yet, but I feel like this is going to be a fast pass.” He acknowledged that it’s “a ways away.”

One way an app could recognize a customer without cameras is geofencing, in which the app uses a phone’s location to detect when a customer enters a zone around the store, as some restaurant chains already do for curbside pickup. Another is a small Bluetooth transmitter at the order board that detects a phone when the car pulls up.

Starbucks hasn’t said publicly how customers would be identified or where the idea would be tested. Responding to an inquiry from GeekWire, Starbucks said Niccol was speaking in the context of the company’s broader effort to make the drive-thru faster, more convenient and more personal, while preserving the interaction between baristas and customers.
“We’re early in this work, and we’ll test, learn, and scale what works,” Niccol said on the call.
Roughly half of Starbucks customers use the drive-thru, he said. Speed matters as Starbucks competes with drive-thru-focused chains such as Dutch Bros and 7 Brew, as Yahoo Finance noted .

Before any fast pass, Starbucks plans to begin testing “background AI models” in its current fiscal year, which began in late September, to help baristas enter orders more accurately and efficiently. The idea builds on a pilot that GeekWire reported on earlier this year , which listens as a customer orders and enters the items into the register automatically.

That approach keeps a person at the speaker, unlike chains that have tried letting AI take the order. McDonald’s ended its AI drive-thru ordering test with IBM in 2024, while Wendy’s has expanded AI ordering nationwide at its drive-thrus using Google Cloud technology.

Starbucks has had its own setbacks with AI in stores. In May, the company retired an AI-powered inventory counting tool built with Redmond, Wash.-based startup NomadGo, just nine months after unveiling it, after baristas reported miscounts and other glitches, as GeekWire reported in July .
“When it fell short, we listened to feedback and changed course,” Starbucks said at the time.

The drive-thru work is part of a broader tech push. Niccol said on the call that the current fiscal year will be “a major tech modernization year,” with new staffing, scheduling and point-of-sale systems rolling out to stores.

The company also plans to begin building delivery directly into the Starbucks app early next year, use AI to improve search in the app and eventually support ordering through AI assistants and from customers’ cars.
Starbucks’ business is picking up, with U.S. same-store sales up 7.7% in the quarter ended Sept. 27.

articles.title: Who gets your vote? What rumors should you spot? Election quiz and bingo offer guidance
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: With Election Day tomorrow, a Seattle-area tech entrepreneur has a quiz to help voters sort through candidates and ballot measures, while University of Washington researchers have a bingo card for spotting familiar election-fraud rumors. Both offer some last-minute perspective — and a little levity.

Mike Dussault , a former SpaceX and Valve engineer and serial startup founder, built Voter Lifeboat , a free quiz designed to help Washington voters identify candidates and ballot-measure positions that align with their values.
“I’m not making money from it,” Dussault said via email. “I built it to help people vote.”

The app asks 17 questions about taxes, climate, housing, data centers and other issues, then generates a report card showing how closely candidates and initiatives align with a user’s answers. The site includes a detailed methodology and links to sources, and users answer the questions anonymously.
The quiz takes just a few minutes, offering another resource alongside traditional voter guides and endorsements from news outlets and other organizations.
Dussault put AI through its paces to build the tool.
“It was fun to task Claude with so much research and reasoning (to vet all the candidates and initiatives) that it maxed out a Claude Ultra subscription,” he said on LinkedIn.

The University of Washington’s Center for an Informed Public (CIP) has served as a watchdog of election-related misinformation for seven years, tracking where it originates and how it spreads online and in the media.
Its Election Rumor Research team this fall created “Rigged Election” Bingo to help people spot recurring conspiracy theories and misleading claims about election fraud.

“Allegedly hacked machines, dead voters, and statistical anomalies are some of the familiar tropes that supposedly ‘prove’ our election system is broken,” the team wrote in a recent post . “These aren’t new ideas.”

Some claims start with real issues, the researchers noted, but exaggerate their scope or omit the safeguards and remedies already in place. The bingo card is designed to help people recognize those patterns and distinguish isolated problems from misleading narratives about the election system.

In Washington, U.S. Attorney Charles Neil Floyd, the top federal prosecutor in Seattle, recently raised allegations of voter fraud . Floyd claimed last month that more than 400 noncitizens had been voting in the state and asked state officials to sequester their ballots.

Secretary of State Steve Hobbs said in a news release that his office was reviewing the allegations and that voter fraud in Washington is “incredibly rare.” He added that the timing of the announcement, a week before the election, “is no doubt intended to cast unfounded suspicion on the results.”

articles.title: Startup uses motion sensors and AI to tell families when an aging parent’s routine changes
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Thessai , a Bellevue, Wash., startup led by a former Microsoft HoloLens executive, is rolling out a home monitoring system for older adults that flags trouble without cameras, microphones or wearables.

Motion sensors placed around the home feed Thessai’s AI software, which learns a person’s normal patterns over time, such as when they wake up, how often they use the bathroom and how much they move around. The system then sends an alert through a mobile app when something falls outside that baseline: a long stretch of inactivity, unusual movement at night, or a front door opening at 2 a.m.

Founder and CEO Michael Nassirian started the company after his mother-in-law fell at home and was injured. She had a phone and an emergency button within reach but didn’t use them, and she told no one until the next day, when she needed an ambulance.

The family looked for a way to keep tabs on her and found only wearables and cameras, which she refused. So Nassirian bought motion sensors at Home Depot, put them around her home, and wrote software to alert his wife if her mother stopped moving.
Keeping quiet about a fall or health scare is common among older adults, Nassirian said.
“Number one, they say, ‘I’m OK.’ Number two, ‘I don’t want to bother you,’” he said. “And number three, and most important, is embarrassment. They do not want to advertise it.”

Pendants and smartwatches with fall alerts have long been the default, but they only help if people use them. A review of nearly 120 fall-detection studies co-authored by a University of Alberta researcher found that older adults who fall often don’t use their devices to reach a caregiver. Thessai joins a crop of companies pitching camera-free ambient monitoring instead, including Cherish , which makes radar-based sensors, and Butlr , which uses thermal heat detection.

Nassirian spent nearly two decades at Microsoft, working on Office, Windows and later HoloLens, where he was a partner quality architect. Before that, he spent about 14 years at Texas Instruments in test engineering. He has a master’s in biomedical engineering from the University of Texas at Austin, and since leaving Microsoft he has founded and advised several startups, including ARVR Academy and Predictive AI Research.

After relatives started asking for monitoring systems of their own, Nassirian formally founded Thessai in 2024 and has self-funded it so far. The company sells two packages, Basic and Premium, to families with an older relative living alone. Its Enterprise package gives senior-living operators a dashboard for monitoring multiple residences.

The Basic package , which includes motion sensors and a hub that plugs into the home’s Wi-Fi, costs $195 plus a $38 monthly subscription. Premium adds features such as a panic button and two-way voice check-ins through the hub, and costs $249 plus $59 a month. The sensors run on batteries that Nassirian said last at least a year and a half.

Nassirian said independent-living communities have been the strongest market so far. Memory-care facilities already have staff watching residents closely, he said, while independent-living operators are pitching Thessai to renters as a “smart home” feature.

Nassirian said the older adult decides what gets monitored. Through the app, they can switch off sensors in certain rooms, the bathroom for example, and limit tracking to the kitchen and living room. Caregivers can also tune alerts to cut down on noise, so a parent who routinely sleeps late, for example, doesn’t set one off.
“We designed it to the last bit of the person’s privacy,” he said.

Thessai is going after a large and growing market. Older adults overwhelmingly want to stay in their homes (75%) and communities (73%), according to AARP’s 2024 Home and Community Preferences Survey , and households led by people 80 and older are set to double by 2040.

The startup soft-launched in May and has a few hundred customers, split between families and senior-care operators, Nassirian said. Its advisory board includes Chuck Lytle, who founded Bellevue-based senior housing companies Lytle Enterprises and Leisure Care.

Nassirian said the company is also working with the Department of Veterans Affairs on bringing the system to veterans, including in rural areas, with the option to run it on the VA’s own secure network.
Thessai has four employees in the U.S. and seven in Singapore. Nassirian is now looking to raise outside money, mainly to buy hardware in larger volumes and bring down per-unit costs.
Longer term, he wants to do away with the physical sensors altogether and detect movement from a home’s existing Wi-Fi signals, an approach researchers at Harvard and Carnegie Mellon are studying.
“I’m in technology,” he said. “I’m not going to sit still.”

articles.title: In Battle with Fire Department, Queen Anne Residents Win Parking Victory
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: A quiet Queen Anne street has become a battleground between the Seattle Fire Department, residents wanting to park their cars, and the simple laws of geometry, but it looks to be Seattle's own parking regulations that have lost the battle – for now.

For decades, there's been an intermittent problem along the upper portion of 14th Avenue W, near Interbay along the west slope of Queen Anne Hill. The street is only around 15 feet wide, narrowing to as little as 14 feet and eight inches. With a row of on-street parking for residents, that isn't usually wide enough for a Seattle Fire Department ladder truck to easily pass through, depending on the exact width of the parked cars. Either the fire truck operator needs to inch their way down 14th to ensure no parked cars get hit, or they need to find another route.

Earlier this year, at the fire department's urging, the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) announced that the street would be entering a new era, with on-street parking prohibited to improve Seattle Fire Department (SFD) response times.

"For every minute we are delayed getting to a fire, roughly that fire doubles in size, and so that increases the risk to you all," Seattle Fire Captain Tim Taylor, based out of Greenwood's Station 21, told Queen Anne residents at a community meeting held on the change this May. "When a rig can't get through or has to try to negotiate a very tight space, those are all things that are going to count directly against patient outcomes. That's the reality that we're dealing with."
Taylor noted that SFD had responded to these specific 14th Avenue blocks 73 times between the beginning of 2022 and this past March.

"We have six documented times where they took the time to send updates to the battalion chiefs and to leadership saying: 'Hey, we had a significant delay due to vehicles blocking and parking on this block,'" Taylor said. "I can tell you, I run into delays quite often. Just traffic or whatever, I don't often take the time to document it. It has to be pretty important for me to take the time to actually send the documentation that we were delayed on a response."

The idea of making parking adjustments to improve public safety might be expected to be non-controversial, but at the May community meeting, the pushback on the change was intense. Residents along 14th repeatedly pressed city staff on finding another path forward, with things turning so combative that one attendee had to be asked to leave after presenting an obscene hand gesture to city staff.
Though the discussion had been arranged to hear residents' concerns about the new parking restrictions, an expectation was laid out at the top: this adjustment was moving forward.
"I do find that it is very important to state at the beginning, this decision is not going to be changed," Rebecca Duran, executive aide to District 7 Councilmember Bob Kettle, told attendees.

And yet, just a few months later, SDOT announced that the decision had in fact been changed. A six-month pilot will evaluate whether vehicles can remain parked on the street "as long as they fit within the available right of way without interfering with reliable emergency vehicle access." A painted line has been added to the length of the street, with signs directing drivers to only park between the line and the curb.

"If your vehicle does not fit the marked area, you can’t park," SDOT's website on the change states. "Together with SFD, we’ll monitor how well the new design supports reliable emergency vehicles’ access. The results will help inform next steps."

On a recent visit to the street, The Urbanist found parked vehicles that were all within the constraints of the painted line on the street – even if that meant that a significant portion of their vehicle was up on the curb. That's also not allowed under the rules of the pilot, which state vehicles have to be 62 inches wide or less to be able to park on the street.
During that May meeting, residents pleaded with the SDOT planner present to essentially grant permission to park on the curb, but were rebuffed.

"The curbs are not actually designed to hold the weight of your vehicle, so you can end up damaging that and the underlaying structure if you park on the wall," SDOT Deputy Transportation Operations Director Matt Beaulieu said that night.

Getting questions answered about how this new parking scheme will be determined to be a success involved a lot of finger pointing within City departments. SDOT referred questions from The Urbanist to the Seattle Fire Department, which then noted that the Seattle Police Department is in charge of parking enforcement.

"Standard parking enforcement practices led by Seattle Police will be in effect. Seattle Fire has no role in enforcement," SFD spokesperson Kim Schmanke wrote. "Seattle Fire will evaluate delays to responses along the route due to access issues and if there were any reported obstructions noted during the non-emergency times."

SPD's parking enforcement division is not as well-resourced as other areas of the police department, with Mayor Katie Wilson recently proposing to eliminate several parking officer positions that had been sitting unfilled for several years. Most of the parking enforcement officer (PEO) resources are focused on areas of the city that have paid parking programs, or in responding to complaints as directed by other officers. With paid parking set to expand to Upper Queen Anne and Alaska Junction, that could mean even less resources for parking enforcement in other areas of the city.

With SFD evaluating response times and SPD maintaining control over enforcement, the pilot appears set up in a way that implicitly condones parking on the curb. But another precedent is potentially being set here, and that concerns SFD's requirements around fire lanes. With some exceptions, Seattle's current fire code requires access roads used by fire department vehicles to have an "unobstructed width" of not less than 20 feet.

But that standard is clearly not being met on 14th Avenue W, which if explicitly acknowledged within City bureaucracy could open the door to more flexible designs elsewhere, clearing a path for greater pedestrianization and traffic calming interventions. In the UK, a fire lane access road is generally only required to be around 12 feet.
"Seattle Fire agreed to this pilot knowing the constraints of the road width and SDOT’s capabilities," Schmanke wrote.

Depending on the way this pilot plays out, the results could have wide-ranging impacts beyond the sleepy confines of 14th Avenue W. For now, drivers will be able to park their cars, regardless of whether doing so involves going up on the curb.

articles.title: Seattle’s oldest Black church delivers ballots on Capitol Hill
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: First African Methodist Episcopal Church , the oldest Black church in Washington state, led a community march to the ballot box on Sunday, marching from the congregation’s 14th Ave home above Capitol Hill to the ballot box on Broadway.

Following services, participants walked half a mile through Capitol Hill to deposit their ballots at Seattle Central College , honoring previous generations while rallying civic engagement ahead of Tuesday’s Election Day.
“Because of their tears, their blood, and their sacrifice, we are now able to do this freely,” said Pastor Carey Anderson , urging younger voters to remember the legacy behind the ballot.
Marchers stressed the impact voting has on the city. “Whatever happens in your daily life is affected by the people who are in charge,” said participant Oveta Hunter .
Fellow marcher Kim Dudley framed participation as an ongoing family responsibility. “We can’t complain if we don’t vote,” she told CHS. “Get out here, take that chance, and vote.”

articles.title: A sour note on E Union: Building issues force closure of Central District’s Meter Music School
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Meter ukelele camp (Image: Meter Music School)

The Central District has lost a music school. After 15 years of guitar, singing, piano, banjo, drums, and ukulele lessons, Meter Music School has shuttered its E Union location as instruction continues at its Columbia City headquarters.
Director Brendan Bosworth confirmed the closure with CHS Monday as the school announced the shutdown to students current and past.

“Our building in the Central District needs major upgrades, so we made the decision to bring all of our programming over to our Columbia City location,” Bosworth said. “It was a wonderful 15 year run on East Union Street.”

Filings with the city show that an annual fire inspection in 2026 raised concerns regarding “unpermitted or non-compliant basement wiring” and structural issues related to unpermitted work on the 1900-era building the music school has called home.

In July, the Seattle Department of Construction & Inspections issued a notice of violation citing the years ago unpermitted conversion work and failure to secure a change of use permit to establish a music institution.

Meter began the pre-application process for working with the city to address the violations but the costs apparently didn’t pencil out for Bosworth or the property’s longtime owners, area real estate investors Charles Ragen and Wenjun Chen .
On Capitol Hill, structural problems and costs around a 96-year-old commercial building on 15th Ave E led to the exit of three businesses in September.

The Meter change will leave a hole in the string of businesses along E Union just west of 23rd and will mean a few changes for area families with young students who have attended in-person instruction at Meter.
In addition to independent instructors, other area options include the School of Rock chain’s studio in Montlake.
Bosworth says Gentle Giant Jiu Jitsu in Madrona has offered to take on the “MiniMeter baby & toddler classes” for area families. Meanwhile, the Columbia City Meter will now operate seven days a week.

articles.title: Targeted for closure during CHOP, city plans $2.2M mechanical upgrade for Capitol Hill’s East Precinct
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: The center of the city’s 2020 unrest over police brutality and a negotiation point in its subsequent “defund” debate, new investments are coming to Capitol Hill’s East Precinct.

Home to the headquarters for the precinct for 40 years, the 109-year-old building is being lined up for a major infrastructure project as the Seattle Police Department prepares to renew its investment in the one-time automobile showroom, service center, and garage at 12th and Pine.

The City of Seattle has completed the pre-application phase for a $2.2 million mechanical overhaul of the building at 1519 12th Ave including its operational patrol headquarters, roll-call and administrative offices, locker rooms, evidence processing areas, and temporary holding cells for officers serving Capitol Hill, First Hill, and the Central District. The stuffed building also supports neighborhood community policing teams and maintains secured, monitored fleet parking for patrol cruisers, police bicycles, and specialized tactical vehicles.
A SPD spokesperson tells CHS the facility will remain open during construction and that “all precinct operations will remain fully functional.”

According to the paperwork, the capital project focuses on modernizing the facility’s heating and ventilation infrastructure to transition away from fossil-fuel heating in compliance with commercial energy codes.

The investment follows uncertainty around the building that first began serving the neighborhood as a showroom for the Wyllis-Overland Company and part of the city’s auto row in 1917. The East Precinct opened at the corner in the 1980s.

Prior to that time, patrol officers covering the precinct were dispatched out of centralized SPD headquarters at the downtown Public Safety Building located between 3rd and 4th Ave and James and Cherry.

Following voter approval to decentralize police stations in 1977, the City of Seattle initially planned to build the East Precinct in the Central District at 23rd and Yesler, but abandoned the plan in 1984 after years of resistance, protests, and a 1981 site occupation led by Black civil rights and community organizers advocating for housing over police infrastructure.

In response, officials selected 12th and Pine as a compromise boundary location serving both Capitol Hill and the Central District, moving forward despite pushback from Capitol Hill queer and progressive activists wary of police harassment, and alongside counter-appeals from local business owners seeking faster response times.
June 2020 brought new scrutiny about the facility as Black Lives Matter protests grew in the city.

The East Precinct’s location placed it directly at the boundary between Capitol Hill’s nightlife and LGBTQ core and the Central District. Barricades outside the station became the nightly standoff site for racial justice marches, with protesters opposing a fortified police presence in a dense arts and residential neighborhood. When police boarded up and evacuated the building on June 8, the precinct became the physical center of the Capitol Hill Autonomous Zone and its walls were covered in art and memorials as demonstrators called for defunding and reallocating police resources.

After the city cleared CHOP four weeks later, the precinct’s future prompted debate over whether a station belonged at 12th and Pine. Officials eventually added a massive but temporary security barrier and continued signing off on repairs and upgrades for the old building.

Following CHOP, community organizers and civil rights groups argued the city should permanently shut it down and turn the site into a community center, echoing the neighborhood battles from the 1970s and 1980s over police facilities in residential areas.

In 2021 , CHS asked the leading candidates for mayor if they would support closing the East Precinct at 12th and Pine. Two said yes and three, including eventual winner Bruce Harrell , said they would consider it.

The new $2.2 million infrastructure project represents a different direction. The work includes removing an old gas boiler and replacing an aging rooftop air handling unit with an electric heat pump system. The upgrade also will add variable air volume terminal boxes across the building and new “Energy Recovery Ventilator Dedicated Outdoor Air Systems” specifically designed to serve the facility’s locker rooms. Work will span across all levels of the structure, including the basement, first- and second-floor interiors, and the roof.

In a typical day, the number of sworn personnel operating out of the East Precinct is split across three 9-hour patrol watches, resulting in a quieter building than the facility’s overall headcount suggests. Out of roughly 75 to 90 total sworn officers and supervisors officially assigned to the precinct, daily street deployment typically translates to just 8 to 14 patrol officers and one or two sergeants on duty per shift to cover the precinct’s sectors. That equates to an average of about 25 to 40 total patrol shifts dispatched from the station across a full day, supplemented by a smaller set of detectives, community liaison officers, and command staff.

Because patrol officers spend the majority of their shifts on the street, on beats, or answering priority calls, the 12th and Pine building itself rarely holds more than 15 to 25 officers at once in brief spikes that occur during morning, afternoon, and late-night watch changes, with the interior settling back down to a front-counter officer and building security for the rest of the day.
The city is getting an early start on the city’s long permit wait times. There is no announced start date for construction.
But, five years later and with 109 years of neighborhood history now having played out inside its building walls, the East Precinct isn’t going anywhere.

articles.title: King County Prosecutor on possible Trump attack on vote-by-mail: ‘We are prepared to respond’
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: King County Elections reports about 30% of ballots have been returned by mail so far

District 3 covering Capitol Hill and the Central District has notched just above a 34% turnout — expect a final surge with younger “late voters” headed for the drop box (Source: King County Elections)
King County’s top lawyer says she is ready to battle in court to protect Seattle voters.

Ahead of Election Day, King County Prosecuting Attorney Leesa Manion highlighted key legal battles her office is leading to protect vote-by-mail systems, voter privacy, and local election administration from federal overreach.

“On the eve of election day, I want to reassure our King County communities that we are closely monitoring any attacks on our election process, and we are prepared to respond with litigation where necessary and appropriate,” Manion said in the announcement.

According to the briefing, Manion joined litigation in *United States Postal Service v. California,* helping secure a Supreme Court order that blocked federal plans to alter mail-in ballot procedures mid-cycle. The proposed rules would have mandated new ballot envelope approvals, unvetted federal portal entries, and in-person postal scanning, potentially disenfranchising voters.
Still, Seattle voters yet to cast a ballot should turn to the county drop boxes at this point to avoid any uncertainty about pick-up and postmarking.
According to King County Elections , around 30% of ballots returned so far have been delivered by mail.

Manion says King County also filed amicus briefs across three multi-state lawsuits resisting Department of Justice demands for complete, unredacted voter-registration records, arguing such orders violate privacy safeguards and overburden local officials.

The efforts are part of a broader defense against federal mandates. Earlier this year, King County and more than 70 local governments prevailed in *King County v. Turner*, where the Ninth Circuit barred the administration from conditioning $364 million in federal grants on anti-DEI, anti-immigrant, and anti-abortion policies.

CHS reported here on the major issues Capitol Hill and Central District voters will decide in Tuesday’s election including the 43rd Legislative District state Senate race between longtime incumbent Jamie Pedersen and challenger Hannah Sabio-Howell , statewide battles over Initiative 001 and Initiative 638 concerning transgender youth, public school policies, and sports, and the proposed Seattle Transit Measure 0.3% sales tax update to expand city bus service and transit access.

There are also some critical judicial branch votes to fill in. Voters in Washington have five nonpartisan State Supreme Court contests on their general election ballot. For Position 1 , sitting state justice Colleen Melody faces private practice attorney Scott Edwards . For Position 3 , King County judge Jaime Michelle Hawk runs against Mason County judge David Stevens . For Position 4 , appeals court judge Ian Birk challenges King County judge Sean O’Donnell . For Position 5 , sitting state justice Theo Angelis faces former municipal judge Dave Larson . Finally, for Position 7 , sitting chief justice Debra Stephens runs against practicing tax attorney Todd Bloom .

All official ballot drop boxes statewide, including the Broadway box , close at 8 PM on Election Night. Voters submitting ballots in person must deposit them before the deadline to ensure they are counted. Details on registration, vote center assistance, and drop box locations are available via King County Elections .

articles.title: Seattle to draft rules requiring side guards on trash and recycling trucks to protect cyclists and pedestrians
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: As it is focusing most of its year-end energy on pounding out the city’s 2027-2028 budget , the Seattle City Council passed a bill last week advancing safety measures aimed at shielding pedestrians and cyclists from fatal side-impact collisions involving large vehicles.

The passage follows the June death of bicyclist Christian Salyer after the Seattle school teacher was struck and killed by the driver of a city contractor recycling truck turning off 12th onto Yesler in June.

Sponsored by Councilmember Rob Saka , the ordinance directs the Department of Finance and Administrative Services with the Seattle Department of Transportation and community stakeholders to draft recommended safety requirements for all city contractors.

Modeled after Boston’s safety standards, the proposed rules will focus on requiring truck side guards which cover the exposed space between a truck’s front and rear wheels to prevent vulnerable road users from slipping underneath.
Officials will also evaluate complementary equipment including convex mirrors and safety decals.
Officials must submit the recommendations to the council by May 1st.

CHS reported here last month as lawyers representing Salyer’s family filed suit against waste contractor Recology and the employee operating the collection truck but did not target the City of Seattle in the wrongful death case.

articles.title: For Some Latino-Owned Businesses, Providing Food Is a Way to Support the South End
paras: For a number of small Latino-owned food businesses, it's been a difficult year. Prices of goods have skyrocketed, and social services that address food insecurity have been squeezed. In the South End, some nonprofits and businesses are feeding people.

Roxana Pardo Garcia is executive director of Alimentando al Pueblo (AAP), a Burien-based nonprofit that provides access to culturally specific Latino foods, economic development, and leadership training. She notes that some small Latino businesses have reported a 40% to 70% drop in profit, in part because of rising costs and increased ICE activity that keep some Latino community members from going out to eat and shop.
AAP and independent Latino businesses have found ways to navigate these times.
AAP started during the COVID-19 pandemic as a Latino food bank. The organization sources 90% of the food it distributes from Latino farms, distributors, grocery stores, and vendors.

Garcia, who grew up in Burien, began to connect with local Latino businesses as a way to invite them to participate in food and monetary donations for AAP's food bank, which serves 500 families in South King County. After understanding more about the struggles of Latino-owned small businesses, Garcia brought together a cohort of businesses that had participated in the programs and offered to support them through the development of branding kits. She also gathered $27,000 in donations and created a voucher system to feed community members. AAP used the money to offer upfront payments to Latino restaurants, cafés, and grocery stores, and then the organization distributed vouchers at their food bank, which people could then spend at designated restaurants and grocery stores.

The cohort of businesses have also created a sheet of coupons that are distributed at their shops and at the AAP food bank. During a campaign called "Comida y Corazón," businesses donated a portion of their sales for six days to AAP, and the organization tabled at the businesses and promoted them. The result has been a connected community of independent Latino businesses and partnership with the food bank.
"The work is rooted in relationship, values, and reciprocity of 'Thank you for showing up for us. We're also showing up for you.'"

Maria and Jasmine Cid are a mother-daughter team who run Café Dulzura in Burien and are part of the AAP cohort. They serve a horchata latte — the recipe was passed down by Maria's mother — and MexiMocha, along with pan dulce, tamales, and more.

Maria recalled that the pan dulces once weren't selling well with customers who didn't speak Spanish, so she considered bringing in croissants or muffins. But instead, she created cards bearing descriptions of the pastries, explaining, for example, that porquitos are traditional Mexican gingerbread. Maria says sales of the pastries then went up.

Maria has noticed changes in how people spend money as the cost of living has increased. "Some people choose to come here over other places because they don't want to see small businesses close. Others say they'll only come once a month now because they don't have as much to spend," she said.

Customers send the Cids information about ICE sightings and safety information for immigrants to pass on to others. "Things like that make me realize how important community is and how the [space] is more than just a coffee shop," said Jasmine. "We're communicating to people about their rights and keeping them informed."

Ay Caramba! Market in Burien is a tidy, midsize grocery with Mexican and Central American staples: rice, beans, tortillas, plantains, spices. It also sells canned vegetables, cookies, chips, and more. The owner, Juan Carlos Sanchez, chats and laughs easily with regular customers. He grew up in South Seattle and worked at his family's grocery store for 10 years before opening Ay Caramba! Market four years ago. "I enjoy helping [people] and sometimes they tell you their stories," said Sanchez. "I'm there to listen."

Sanchez has noticed how increased costs for items like canned goods and detergents affect customers. "Sometimes they come with coins. Sometimes their card is declined, and I notice their reaction," Sanchez said.
He says that if someone is picked up by ICE, people tend to avoid the area where the action occurred because they worry ICE may return, which impacts nearby businesses.

Sanchez participated in AAP's food-bank fundraising campaign, and he donated 5% of all sales for six days to the organization. Sanchez says he found the campaign brought him more business since AAP promoted the campaign and the participating businesses . Sanchez says he's connected closely with other Burien businesses from the campaign. "I don't feel alone. I feel support not just from Alimentando al Pueblo, but from the rest of the businesses. We exchange ideas and check on each other," said Sanchez.

Karen Sandoval and Cesar Martinez started Bakescapade in a commercial kitchen in Burien four years ago. Sandoval, who grew up in Beacon Hill, attended culinary school and worked as a baker and a pastry chef before starting Bakescapade. She says she missed the concha she ate while visiting her extended family in Mexico City. "All the places I worked had been American, Italian, or French," said Sandoval. "I wanted my baked goods to tell about me — my Mexican heritage, growing up in Washington, and celebrating the holidays I've grown up with."
She creates seasonal pastries, like a strawberry shortcake or blueberry cobbler concha in summer and apple pie or lemon curd concha in fall.

Sandoval doesn't have a brick-and-mortar shop, so instead she creates seasonal pastries for coffee shops. "I want more people to be intrigued by Mexican cuisine. It's an honor to be able to highlight my culture and community, especially during these times," Sandoval said.
Grumpy Bean for savory empanadas Seattle Children's Research Institute Building, 910 Stewart St., Seattle Westlake Tower lobby, 1601 5th Ave., Seattle

Karina Arroyo and Rita Manalastas, founders of Big Bush Co. , started their Mexipino baked-goods company in January as a cottage business out of their Des Moines, Washington, home. Their journey as bakery owners began last year when their dog had expensive veterinary bills. The couple paid down the expenses with a bake sale where Manalastas sold more than 100 loaves of banana bread.

The two continued their baking exploration of Arroyo's Mexican heritage and Manalastas' Filipino roots by creating treats, like cochinitos (pig-shaped gingerbread pastries), calamansi muffins and ube muffins, and cultural mashups, like a concha with a crust flavored with Kopiko, Southeast Asian coffee candy. The two were recently featured as Emerging Makers Fellows in Residence at Anh Ơi Bakeshop . They participated in an AAP campaign earlier this year where they hosted a Latino food drive at pop-ups and offered free mini-conchas for anyone who contributed.

Arroyo says her father moved to the U.S. from Oaxaca several decades ago, and his family managed the only stone oven in the town where he grew up. He told her he'd "see people from their pueblo leading up to Dia de los Muertos baking pan de muerto in their family's stone oven throughout the day, so they could place the bread on their ofrendas at home," said Arroyo. "[My grandfather] passed away a couple of years ago, so he'll be part of my ofrenda this year. It feels really special to know that he was a baker, just like me."

articles.title: Oops! All Ghosts!
articles.author: Megan Burbank
paras: The Nutcracker may be canonically known as the official ballet of holiday hell, but not enough of us are acquainted with the rich Venn diagram that exists between classical ballet and Spooky Season, from the undead brides of Giselle to the baroque body horror of Suspiria . So I am delighted to report that Pacific Northwest Ballet’s second production of its current season could easily be called “Oops! All Ghosts!” if artistic director Peter Boal was more of a jokester. (Sorry, Peter Boal! I know joking is not allowed in ballet!) Ghost Stories , which opens November 6 , promises “a gaggle of goosebumps,” and features a Whitman’s Sampler’s worth of Halloween treats, from a George Balanchine weird-girl classic to a new Edgar Allan Poe adaptation choreographed by PNB principal dancer Kyle Davis.

For those who aren’t already ballet-pilled, Ghost Stories promises to be a fun way in. Compared with the hours-long commitment of a story ballet like Swan Lake (which is arguably very spooky in its own bird-person way ), a variety pack evening like this one is a great entry point if you’re new to watching ballet. In Ghost Stories , you’re going to get something weird, something new, and something rooted in American ballet tradition.

The latter shows up in my favorite fractured bedtime story, La Sonnambula , a goth-coded confection perfect for girls who are just sooooooo sleepy. Though the story is ostensibly about a doomed poet’s romantic troubles (who cares), the real MVP of La Sonnambula is a mysterious sleepwalker (relatable) who haunts the stage in a glorious, vaguely 1970s-doing-Victorian nightgown, while brandishing a candlestick. I saw this ballet for the first time as a teenager and found it incredibly chic and odd. I’m not always a fan of Balanchine (please don’t hurt me!), but La Sonnambula is one of his finer projects, and perfect Halloween-adjacent viewing, especially if you care deeply about Alvin Schwartz books like Scary Stories to Tell in the Dark and In a Dark, Dark Room and Other Scary Stories (I’m thinking mostly of the one about the girl with the ribbon around her neck), the Brontë sisters (more Emily, less Charlotte, no Emerald Fennell), or the Mia Goth cinematic universe.

PNB principal Davis cares deeply about Edgar Allan Poe’s famous, brief account of a visitation from a “grim, ungainly, ghastly, gaunt, and ominous bird of yore”—so much that it’s the inspiration for his new ballet The Raven . Menacing tales of animal encounters are perfect source material for classical dance, but Davis’s effort to track down the music for this piece is equally compelling: He wanted to use Alexander Dreyschock’s Morceau de concert , Op. 27, a semi-forgotten piece of music that had been recorded only twice and whose sheet music seemed not to exist. Following a decades-long odyssey involving both the Festival of Neglected Romantic Music (yes, it’s real) and the smarts of PNB music librarian Mona Butler, Davis located the only copy of the score known to exist. It’s since been copied, and will accompany Davis’s take on Poe’s legendary poem. (There’s even a Poe dress-up night during the run. What is this, the Independence Inn?)

The final ghost on the lineup trades narrative for something closer to abstraction in Alejandro Cerrudo’s Silent Ghost and PACOPEPEPLUTO . Cerrudo’s ballets have a cheeky contemporary charm—my favorite is Little mortal jump , a ballet featuring music by Andrew Bird and getting-stuck-on-a-wall choreography. With its moody partnering and emotional palette, Silent Ghost fits the evening’s brief perfectly. But it’s hard to make the case that PACOPEPEPLUTO is a ghost story, unless it’s about the ghost of Dean Martin. It kind of doesn’t matter, though, because this piece, which premiered at Chicago’s Hubbard Street Dance in 2011, is a real winner: a winsome, campy series of male solos set to classics like “That’s Amoré.” If The Raven conjures foggy, consumptive supernatural horror, PACOPEPEPLUTO is a welcome diversion to Palm Springs, the choreographic equivalent of a poolside cocktail garnished with a sparkly umbrella. It’s fun. It has a sense of humor. Sometimes joking is allowed in ballet.
See Ghost Stories November 6–15 at McCaw Hall .

articles.title: Stranger Suggests: Your Agenda This Week, November 2–8
articles.author: Julianne Bell, Amanda Manitach, Charles Mudede, Dave Segal, Meg van Huygen, and Audrey Vann
paras: (FILM) This anthology film is based on four Japanese ghost stories collected in a book by the Greek/Irish writer Lafcadio Hearn, who spent the last part of his life in a Japan that was rapidly modernizing due to the Meiji Restoration (1889-1912). Hearn’s Kwaidan: Stories and Studies of Strange Things was published in 1904; Kobayashi’s film was released in 1964. The latter is, to be honest, far better than the former because, again to be honest, Hearn was not a great writer, but Kobayashi was one of the masters of post-war Japanese cinema. The first film in the anthology, “The Black Hair,” has a stimmung and sets whose beauty is almost supernatural. ( SIFF Cinema Downtown, 6 pm ) CHARLES MUDEDE

(FILM) When Ken Russell’s film The Devils came out in 1971, it was met with intense controversy because of its portrayal of sex and violence and anti-religious themes, garnering it an X rating (since updated to NC-17). 55 years later, it’s now being re-released in a new 4k restoration that puts all its horny, shocking glory on full display. Oliver Reed stars as the original hot priest, Father Urbain Grandier, who is accused of witchcraft for simply being too sexy. Vanessa Redgrave plays the sexually repressed mother superior Sister Jeanne des Anges, who becomes fixated on Grandier to the point of sparking an outbreak of fake hysteria and “demonic possessions” among the convent’s nuns. Massive orgies, frenzied masturbation with crucifixes, and public executions ensue! ( SIFF Cinema Downtown, 4 pm ) JULIANNE BELL

(MUSIC) Band reformations featuring only one original member should always draw skepticism—such as this one with drummer Jody Stephens representing Memphis power-pop legends Big Star. Would you really want to see Ringo performing Beatles songs with a pick-up group of acolytes? Wait… Anyway, Big Star should’ve been at least half as popular as the Beatles, but instead they’ve become perhaps the ultimate cult rock unit. Led by guitarist/vocalists Alex Chilton and Chris Bell, Big Star released three studio albums that abound with ebullient, earworm-heavy rockers and heart-melting ballads. I’ve listened to #1 Record (1972), Radio City (1974), and 3rd (1978) hundreds of times without tiring of their brilliance, and I’m far from alone. For this tour, Mike Mills, Jon Auer, Pat Sansone, and Chris Stamey join Stephens in reanimating Big Star’s timeless tunes. ( Neptune Theatre, 8 pm, all ages ) DAVE SEGAL

(VISUAL ART) Curated by tom manzanarez, I Am Love: Rituals in Resistance stems from a broader project ( I Am Love ) aimed at forming new connections and providing platforms for queer artists in the PNW through exhibitions, workshops, and other opportunities. It’s only continued to grow since its inception, and this month’s exhibit at RailSpur offers a window onto the region’s multidimensional, robust queer scene. Objects like Michael Espinoza’s pairing of embroidery with i-Type Polaroids exemplify the kind of work that’s both conceptually rigorous and intimate, dexterously touching on themes of domesticity and ephemerality. (Have you ever seen a print transfer applied to a slice of processed cheese product? The poetics of the show will surprise you.) ( RailSpur ) AMANDA MANITACH

(MUSIC) When Corin Tucker’s pre-Sleater-Kinney band with Tracy Sawyer, Heavens to Betsy, announced their first show in 32 years, they did it the old-fashioned way: by plastering fliers around Portland. Nevertheless, the show sold out almost immediately, and I, all the way in Seattle, was seething with envy. The 1994 album Calculated is one of my most treasured pieces of music and my favorite to come out of the riot grrrl movement, and it soundtracked so many angry walks through my high school hallway. When Tucker shouts, “I’m going crazy, do you wanna watch? Do you wanna come?” on the lyrically and sonically seething “Axemen,” I felt that in my bones. Luckily for me, the duo has since announced a reunion tour with a stop at Neumos alongside Olympia-based psychedelic-rock band Nudity. ( Neumos, 7 pm, 21+ ) AUDREY VANN

(MUSIC) As you may have heard, Freakout announced back in May that their annual psychedelic festival isn’t returning this year. Thankfully, Baba Yaga has stepped in with their own new Baba Obscura festival, which is not associated with Freakout, but fills the psilocybin mushroom-shaped hole in the heart of Seattle. The four-day, six-venue festival will feature big-name acts, like the Black Angels (who are celebrating the 20th anniversary of Passover ), post-punk trio Provoker, Nigerien rock guitarist Mdou Moctar, Portland alt-country stars Rose City Band, psych-rock outfit Black Mountain, and garage-rock revivalists the Gories. There are also plenty of local favorites on the lineup, including Dark Chisme, the Black Tones, Zookraught, and Linda From Work. ( Various venues, times vary ) AUDREY VANN

(FOOD) If you’re new to Seattle, attending a festival at precious little Dom Polski, aka Polish Home Association, is mandatory to becoming a local. The Polish Fall Bazaar is the less-crowded version of Dom Polski’s Pierogi Fest in the summer. Much more chill, more diverse dishes, and the food is always the tiiiiiits: pierogis, pickle soup, white borscht, cabbage rolls, crêpes, baked goods like pączki and poppyseed cake, pyzy and other Polish dumplings of variety, and so on. Upstairs, there’s imported Polish stuff for sale: kielbasa, frozen dumplings, amber jewelry, and beeyoootiful hand-painted Bolesławiec pottery. They’ll be raffling off baskets of Polish treats as well. Admission is free, but bring lots of snack money. ( Dom Polski, noon–5 pm, all ages ) MEG VAN HUYGEN

(FILM) I am obsessed with vintage erotica, and not for the reason you probably think. Back in the 1960s and ’70s, directors of pornographic films had an equal dedication to erotic visuals as to artistic integrity. The result is a movement of psychedelic softcore porn films with some of the most beautiful costumes, soundtracks, and cinematography I’ve ever seen (see: Just Jaeckin’s The Story of O , Radley Metzger’s The Lickerish Quartet , and Walerian Borowczyk’s Immoral Tales ). Seattle Erotica Cinema Society is dedicated to preserving this movement of artistic blue movies with their annual film festival, SECS Fest, screening both old and new artsy, innovative, and often queer erotic films that range from straight-up porn to softcore, sexploitation, art films, and sexy experimental works. Highlights from this year’s program include the 1981 campy feminist erotic film, Outlaw Ladies , the 2025 documentary The Story of James Bidgood (and the Making of Pink Narcissus) , and plenty of saucy short films. ( Beacon Cinema, 2 pm and 4 pm ) AUDREY VANN

articles.title: Slog AM: Michigan Democrat Excommunicated, a Puppets’ Viral Candy Machine, Man Walks Around World and Returns 28 Years Later
articles.author: Cedar Attanasio
paras: The midterms are here and I’m stress eating and figuring out who to blame if Democrats don’t tsunami The Hill. If we haven’t voted yet, and haven’t gotten our cousins in Michigan and Texas to do so, it’s on us. My ballot got delivered to an old address, so I’ll be heading to my local voting center for a replacement tomorrow.
In Washington, Gov. Bob Ferguson is voting in an official ballot box. He suggests putting your ballot in a drop box to avoid any Trumpification of mail delivery.
Looking for The Stranger Election Control Board 2026 General Election Cheat Sheet ? It’s here .

In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed’s defeated Democratic rival endorsed his Republican opponent. Former Democratic Congresswoman Haley Stevens betrayed her party over the weekend by endorsing Republican Mike Rogers against the most thoughtful, inspiring Democratic candidate for Senate since Barack Obama. Democrats from Chuck Schumer to Michigan’s state party chair essentially excommunicated her over the “despicable betrayal,” The Associated Press reports. Which reminds me, how did Jill Biden avoid this treatment, after her own betrayal to the Democratic Party? Trump called Stevens brave, and invited her to join the Republican party. If ever there were a clear test to see if AIPAC can buy a senate seat, this is it.

In Alaska, a court rejects Trump’s “Dan Sullivan lawsuit.” A federal judge has tossed a Department of Justice (DOJ) lawsuit that sought to prevent Alaska from certifying its Senate election results… if the Republican candidate lost, NPR reports . Trump personally ordered the lawsuit, another unprecedented form of election interference and weaponization of the DOJ. The lawsuit accurately went after an apparent stunt from Democratic operatives to recruit a man named Dan J. Sullivan to run against the sitting Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, who has a different middle initial. Alaskan officials (including top Republicans) are investigating the move, but have also rejected Trump’s attempt to hijack the results.

Don’t blame the amoral Democratic operatives who recruited the other Dan Sullivan. Ya, they’re a bunch of assholes. But it turns out their biggest mistake was getting caught. Republicans also tried to manipulate the state’s open primary by funding a Green Party candidate, but it didn’t work out, NPR reports . And who could forget when there were three Bob Fergusons on the Washington ballot in 2024?

When will we know midterm election results? Slowly, PolitiFact reports . Ignore the noise, stay off Truth Social, and wait for a call from AP. When they’re in, Alaska’s Dan Sullivan—the Republican incumbent—says he’ll respect them, even if the President doesn’t, CNBC says .

The insurance is too damn high: Individual insurance premiums will increase by more than 22 percent on average in 2027, the Seattle Times reports . It’s the third year in a row that rates have gone up by double-digits in Washington.

The refrigerators are too damn hot: Industrial cooling fridges in supermarkets across Europe got hacked again . This happened in France last month, with software sending grocery store refrigerators into hot mode, and looks like the hack got scaled up this time. Hackers targeted fridges and freezers at stores in Sweden, the Netherlands, Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Estonia.

Eating our way out of a problem: La Palma Family Mexican Restaurant in Ballard, which was on the verge of closure, is bouncing back after a social media plea asking for help went viral, KOMO reports . If social media says so, I may take a break from my nightly frozen TJ’s meals to eat at La Palma. As a native New Mexican, I have been hate-eating my way around Seattle’s Latin food scene. Hopefully it is better than Trader Jose’s green chile bowl, which I can’t say for Taco Time.

A few weeks ago I stood at this podium and declared that Grimothy, the Bainbridge horror installation, had won Halloween. I was wrong. Behold, Eggy , the puppet in Columbia City that distributed candy through a giant machine. He described himself as a former Sesame Street writer who never got on camera. He gave children candy.

Dad went out to get a pack of cigarettes… for 28 years: In 1998 a recently divorced UK dad left his eight year old son to literally walk around the world, because therapy had not yet been invented for men. Karl Bushby, 57, hugged his mum on Monday after completing the round-the-world journey, The Guardian reported. He was also reunited with his son, now 36, and got to meet his 12-year-old granddaughter. In tow was German film-maker Werner Herzog, who is making a movie about the walk.
A year before he set out, “Around The World” was released. Daft Punk may ultimately be responsible for planting a seed in Bushby’s brain by releasing their Magellenesque single.

articles.title: Procrastinators, there’s still time to register and vote in WA
articles.author: Lizz Giordano
paras: Election Day is upon us. Haven’t registered yet? No worries, you’ve still got time. In Washington, you can actually walk in, register, and vote the same day, right up until 8 p.m. on Election Day.

Even before election day, machines have been scanning ballots for days at King County election headquarters in Renton. Every ballot from King County voters takes a pass around the second floor of this building as workers verify and scan each one.
Downstairs, things get busy too. In the days leading up to an election, the first-floor elections center fills up with last-minute voters coming in to register and cast their ballot.

“By law, we do have to lock those drop boxes and close those vote center doors at 8 p.m. But if you are in line for either of those things, you will still get to vote and your ballot will be on time. So folks can come right up until that 8 p.m. deadline,” said Kendall Hodson, Chief of Staff of King County Elections. “Of course, we'd certainly recommend coming a little bit earlier. We will probably see some lines. It also is just good peace of mind to make sure you get that ballot in. But yeah, if you are a procrastinator, we are still going to help you as long as you're in line by 8.p.m.”
There are seven election centers in King County where voters can still register on Election Day and vote that day. Voters can also come for a replacement ballot or if they have other questions.
Each county has at least one election center open until 8pm election night. Visit the Washington Secretary of State’s website to find an election center.
Hodson says folks don’t need to bring anything with them to register to vote.

“All they need is themselves. It's helpful if they have their Washington State ID with them or driver's license, is great. If they know their social security number, the last four digits is going to be helpful as well,” Hodson said

paras: We cannot let the billionaire class take unprecedented risks with our future

articles.title: ‘Screams on the level of a Taylor Swift concert’: horny romp Wicker gets the 4DX treatment
articles.author: Adrian Horton
paras: Olivia Colman’s steamy romance, where she plays a woman in love with a wicker man, becomes an unlikely pick for the theme park-like cinema experience
What does Olivia Colman’s hot sex with a basket tell us about heteropessimism?
‘I saw the script and went: oooh!’ Olivia Colman and Alexander Skårsgard on their steamy folk-horror movie Wicker

Since its introduction in the US in 2014, 4DX, the rollercoaster-ization of the theatrical experience, has primarily been the purview of action movies. And for good reason; the high-speed chases of a Fast and Furious movie, or repetitive battle sequences of an Avatar saga, translate easily to the moving chairs, scent machines and wind/water sprayers of the format, which more closely resembles an amusement park ride than cinema.

As a longtime fan of plane turbulence-style seat movement, I thought the immersive pleasures of 4DX – the second most-popular of so-called large premium formats in the US, behind Imax – reached its zenith in the summer of 2024 with the release of Twisters, a perfectly fine action movie about tornadoes that became an 11/10 experience when jostled in one’s seat to actual wind and rain. But a recent, unexpected candidate is finally pushing the bounds of 4DX again, making the most of the format’s potential to enhance the sensorial joys of cinema.

articles.title: Not in a FEMA flood zone? Your home could still be at risk – and you could suffer more than your neighbor
articles.author:
<name>Yilei Yu, Senior Researcher and Postdoctoral Fellow in Geography, Rice University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/yilei-yu-2644325"/>
paras: If your home isn’t in a federally designated flood zone, flooding might seem like someone else’s problem. No one requires you to buy flood insurance, and the map suggests you’re in the clear. But reality may be very different.

Mounting evidence reveals that significantly more homes are at risk of flooding than is indicated by FEMA’s 100-year flood maps – about 6 million more , and 14.6 million properties in all, by one estimate. The official maps are commonly outdated , and some are two decades old . Even when updated, they typically rely on historical flood data rather than future risk projections.
But there’s another problem that redrawing the lines won’t solve.
FEMA’s flood maps answer only one question: Is the water likely to reach my neighborhood? They don’t assess an individual home’s risks or what the impacts are likely to be when the water rises.
To understand the impact, more comprehensive data is needed , including the probable flood depth at the home, the building’s age and construction quality, and insurance coverage.
When these other factors are considered, your home’s true flood risk is far more complex than the map might seem to indicate.
The data shows how two houses on the same street can face radically different risks from flooding , even when located in the same flood zone – and where local governments can help.

One home may be newer, well maintained and covered by flood insurance. Another may be decades older, at the low end of the same street where water runs deeper during a flood, and is in poor repair and uninsured. The same storm would leave them in very different predicaments, with very different paths to recovery.

Neighborhood averages can make it hard to tell which homes are likely to be hit hardest. But understanding an individual property’s risks matters for residents figuring out how to protect a home, and for local officials deciding where limited flood-protection money should go.

We study how flooding affects homes and the people who live in them. To see how much these house-by-house differences matter, we and colleagues Aaron Flores of Arizona State University and Sara Meerow of the University of Colorado Boulder built a detailed flood risk score for nearly 1 million homes in Houston. We describe the results in a new study published in the journal Applied Geography.

Our past research in Houston found that more than half of 100,000 documented flood-prone buildings in the city currently lie outside official flood boundaries, and that these overlooked buildings are more likely to be in poor condition and uninsured, leaving them especially exposed when the floodwaters do come.
The new research helps communities locate those homes.
To get a better understanding of each household’s vulnerability, we combined four types of information about each home.

We chose these four criteria because flood research consistently highlights their importance for how hard a flood hits a community: how much water arrives , how well the building holds up , whether people can still get around and how big the repair bill is for the owner . They aren’t the only possible measures; a city could use others within each category, depending on available data.

Homes in the same neighborhood can have very different flood vulnerability scores. In fact, we found the scores differed more from house to house within a neighborhood than from one neighborhood to the next.

In practice, this means that knowing a neighborhood’s flood risk doesn’t necessarily tell you how hard a flood could hit any individual home. A neighborhood could look safe on average while containing some of the county’s riskiest homes , and there may be many well-protected homes in an otherwise risky neighborhood. Much of the problem, we show, lies at the scale of buildings, not neighborhoods or ZIP codes.
Homeowners can check several of these risks themselves.

Ask longtime neighbors or your city’s flood plain office whether your home or the street has been flooded before. Look up the home’s age in local property records and have an inspector assess its condition. Find out whether the routes to work and school flood easily. And check whether you have a flood insurance policy , and what it covers: Most homeowner’s policies don’t cover flood damage.

Communities can apply our approach with their own data to locate particularly vulnerable housing where neighborhood averages may disguise the need for help. They can start with existing address-level flood scores, such as First Street’s , and add local records on buildings, roads and insurance. The extra details matter because officials have limited money for flood-proofing homes , improving drainage and helping families recover after floods. Better data on buildings and flood risk can help them invest wisely.
Data similar to that used for Houston exists across much of the United States, so other flood-prone cities could follow the same approach.
Floods don’t stop at the lines on a map, and they don’t hit every house on a street the same. We believe it’s time for residents and local flood authorities to prepare accordingly.

articles.title: Disaster aid has become a political lottery – libraries, schools and places of worship are stepping into the breach
articles.author:
<name>Daniel P. Aldrich, Professor of Political Science, Public Policy and Urban Affairs, Northeastern University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/daniel-p-aldrich-318874"/>
paras: Four tornadoes tore across southwest Michigan in early March 2026, killing four people. They were the state’s deadliest natural hazards in decades .
Gov. Gretchen Whitmer asked the Federal Emergency Management Agency for assistance to cover uninsured and underinsured losses. FEMA said no. She appealed. FEMA said no again .

I study how communities prepare for and recover from disasters. As Dean’s Professor of Resilience at Northeastern University , I have written six books on the topic, including the forthcoming “ Beyond Common Ground .”
The fact that Michigan was repeatedly denied aid reflects a broader shift, one that is putting more weight on the ties between neighbors and the places where they meet.
The Trump administration denied 26% of major disaster declarations in 2025, more than double the rate of the year before and well above the 15% denial average of the past two decades.

Denials have not fallen evenly. One study looked at some 2,500 disaster declarations since FEMA’s creation in 1979 in states where the governor and U.S. senators were all Republican or all Democrat. In his second term, Trump approved nearly 90% of requests from all-Republican states while approving only 23% of those from all-Democratic states .
Colorado, an all-Democratic state, had both of its 2025 appeals for disaster rejected. They were Colorado’s first denials since the 1980s .

Florida, an all-Republican state, fared differently. In June, Trump announced US$416 million for the state’s disasters without specifying which one, adding that much of it would go to the Panhandle, one of his “favorite places .” There, a January 2025 snowstorm was linked to 13 deaths and caused approximately $200 million in damages.

Nationally, an analysis of FEMA data by Andrew Rumbach, a senior fellow at the Urban Institute, found that about 84% of requests from states Trump won in 2024 were approved during his second term, compared with about 42% from states he lost .

While the White House has denied that politics plays a role in who receives aid after shocks, local communities are now shouldering more of the cost of preparing for, responding to and recovering from disasters than they did before 2025.

FEMA owes local governments almost $10 billion in reimbursements for recovery work that cities and towns have already paid for. When a declaration is denied, towns can be left covering costs as high as 15% of their annual budget . Philanthropies and aid groups such as Team Rubicon are expanding their roles to fill the gaps.
Nonprofits and community organizations cannot replace federal funding, but they can build cooperation, trust and collective action , which can better prepare neighborhoods and accelerate recovery.
In Union City, Michigan, help arrived within hours of the EF3 tornado that killed three people in March 2026. It came not from Washington but from neighbors.
School administrators turned the local high school into a shelter the night of the storm, volunteers arrived with food and supplies, and the local United Way opened a relief fund.
That is typical: Local residents are almost always the first responders after disasters strike. What was different is that federal help never followed.

Donations poured into the local high school, and the superintendent said staff worked out how to get supplies to the people who needed them . A local church, damaged in the storm, started a disaster fund to help residents pay their insurance deductibles .
Research on U.S. disasters shows how places such as schools, faith-based organizations and libraries can keep communities knit together.

After Hurricane Katrina in August 2005, floodwaters as high as 12 feet (3.6 meters) covered the low-income neighborhood around the Mary Queen of Vietnam Church in east New Orleans. Yet by summer 2007, about 90% of its residents had returned to their homes. For the city as a whole, the figure hit only 45% . The difference was likely the leadership of the Rev. Vien Nguyen, who coordinated supplies, organized volunteers and kept scattered residents in touch even as they evacuated to other states.

My lab’s research during the COVID-19 pandemic found a similar pattern. We compared U.S. counties that were alike in many ways but differed in their social ties. After accounting for politics, governance, healthcare quality and demographics, our study found that two kinds of ties reduced the pandemic’s toll : bonding ties and linking ties.
Bonding ties connect neighbors and family.
Linking ties connect residents to officials. Those ties are often built through spaces designed for connection, such as libraries and faith-based organizations like Nguyen’s church in New Orleans.
Libraries continue to safeguard our most vulnerable. In 2025, 44.7% of U.S. public libraries served as cooling or warming centers during extreme temperatures, up 8.2% from 2022 .

Many could do more. In a national survey, 84% of library directors agreed that libraries have a critical role in disaster response. Yet only 36% knew that federal law allows libraries to seek FEMA relocation funding to move to safer ground, and just 51% had an emergency preparedness plan .

In my new book , I show that more than 90% of federal disaster funds went to roads, utilities and other standard infrastructure in the early 21st century, and less than 10% to libraries, parks, schools, places of worship and community centers, where neighbors check on one another and organize recovery.
Federal aid may go to rebuild some of these spaces, but it rarely pays to keep them open and running when communities need them most.

In another study, I found that Japanese communities with higher density of social infrastructure had half the number of deaths from a catastrophic tsunami in March 2011 compared to similar communities with fewer gathering spaces .

In my assessment, as federal aid becomes less predictable, these kinds of places people frequent often will have to carry us into the future. The communities that recover best from the next disaster may be the ones that kept their libraries open, their civic halls full of volunteers and their parks full of residents.
