articles.title: Students who attended Miami-Dade public school pre-K outperformed peers in 18-year study
articles.author:
<name>Charles Bleiker, Associate Professor of Early Childhood Education, Florida International University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/charles-bleiker-2747016"/>
paras: Choosing a preschool is a difficult and important decision. Parents are weighing cost, proximity and convenience with how each program meets the needs of the child and matches the goals and values of their family and cultural community.

This choice makes a difference. Research in early education clearly shows that children who attend high-quality preschool programs – those with smaller class sizes, a developmentally appropriate curriculum, warm teacher-child interactions and established, efficient routines – are better prepared for kindergarten .

We are researchers who study early childhood education , and we conducted an 18-year study tracking the academic progress of 27,814 students who attended different types of prekindergarten in Miami and then went on to attend the Miami-Dade County Public Schools system from kindergarten through high school. We found that the type of pre-K program the children attended made a difference for their overall educational outcomes.

From 2002 to 2007, we partnered with Miami-Dade County Public Schools, early childcare providers across the county and the Early Learning Coalition of Miami-Dade , a nonprofit that works with childcare providers and communities to promote school readiness, with the goal of assessing five cohorts of about 10,000 students per year.

School readiness takes into consideration the children’s cognitive, language, motor and social skills, as well as behavior problems. During the study, we shared the data we collected with parents, teachers and center directors to inform interventions for struggling kids and improvements to their pre-K programs.

Some of the students in these five cohorts attended taxpayer-funded, public school pre-K programs, while some received federal subsidies administered through the state of Florida to attend center-based or family childcare at age 4.

Center-based programs, like a Kiddie Academy, for example, can be nonprofit or for-profit centers in the community. They operate either in a freestanding location or as part of a corporate or faith-based building. Family or home-based childcare programs are generally smaller and operate out of private residences.

After the children had moved through pre-K, we continued to receive their anonymized academic records each year, as long as they stayed in the public school system. The last cohort of students completed 12th grade in spring 2020.

We found that children who attended public school pre-K programs at age 4 achieved the strongest third-grade outcomes on standardized reading and math test scores and GPA. These children outperformed those who attended center-based care, who in turn generally performed better than children who were enrolled in family childcare. Kids who attended public school pre-K were 35% less likely to be held back in third grade compared with the other groups.
Further, we found that kids who attended higher-quality elementary schools – as measured by the Florida Department of Education – did better on average.

However, the quality of the elementary school that students went on to attend didn’t change the differences we observed across the early childhood education types, except when it came to reading skills. Students who attended center-based care and went on to attend higher-quality schools were better able to catch up to the public school pre-K kids by third grade in reading.

Our findings are consistent with most previous studies of public pre-K. Students who attended public pre-K programs in Boston ; Tulsa, Oklahoma ; and North Carolina have shown better results on standardized test scores, lower absenteeism and better grade retention when compared with children who attended other programs, even as late as eighth grade.

However, there are outliers. Children who attended the publicly funded voluntary pre-K program in Tennessee did not perform any better than other children on third or sixth grade outcomes – and in some cases, they performed worse.
Previous findings are also mixed on whether these effects persist past the third grade .

In our study, it appears that the long-term benefits of public school pre-K extend through eighth grade, but this conclusion is still in peer review and has not been published yet. We are currently examining whether benefits persist throughout high school.

Why did kids in public school pre-K programs do better compared to center-based and family childcare? We believe that the answer likely lies in the quality and organizational differences between the three different types of early care and education.

The public school pre-K programs in our study benefited from the collective resources of the fourth-largest public school system in the country. This matters for everything from the quality of teachers they are able to hire to the facilities and curriculum.

Miami-Dade public schools require teachers to have at minimum a bachelor’s degree and a teaching credential, whereas the others required less education at the time of our study. Public pre-K teachers’ certification allows them to teach from pre-K to third grade, so they typically bring their experience of teaching in kindergarten and the early elementary grades to the pre-K classroom.

These programs also used a developmentally appropriate curriculum, while the others used a variety of materials and approaches. When we began this study, the center-based programs were mostly independent, unaffiliated sites, although some for-profits had more than one center in the study, and some nonprofit organizations such as Catholic Charities or the YMCA oversaw multiple centers.

Many of the children in the study moved from one school to another within the same district. Because Miami-Dade’s public schools are part of a countywide system, the children’s academic records moved with them easily, so their new teacher could see their progress. And since the curriculum was the same across the district, the students were able to pick up at their new school where they’d left off.

This continuity could also explain why children who entered the public school system in pre-K performed better than those outside it. The majority of the children in the study went on to attend public elementary school. The kids in public school preschool and their parents were therefore already familiar with the schools that they would be attending the following year. It’s not hard to see how this would be an advantage for a child transitioning from preschool to kindergarten.

Our findings do not indicate to us, however, that every child must attend public school pre-K in order to succeed in school later on. The reality in Miami-Dade County – and in most communities – is that we need all forms of early care and education, and each setting serves important needs for families.

Indeed, students in all three types of programs made excellent school readiness gains from the beginning to the end of the age-4 academic year. It was just that the children in the public school preschools made stronger gains.

Center- and home-based care in Miami-Dade County is much higher quality across the board today than when we began our study back in 2002. Many more centers are accredited, and teacher education levels have improved. In fact, in our assessment, the quality of early education in Miami-Dade County has never been better .

Still, the cohesive system offered by public schools remains the gold standard for preschool when serving most children and families. In terms of teacher preparation and qualifications, standardized curriculum, oversight and alignment with the kindergarten curriculum, public school pre-k for low-income families in Miami still offers the best hope of long-term academic success.

articles.title: Getting a big head start on holiday shopping can benefit retailers and consumers alike
articles.author:
<name>James Malm, Professor of Finance and Director of the Global Business Resource Center, College of Charleston</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/james-malm-2682174"/>
paras: Amazon, Costco, Target, Walmart and other retailers begin their holiday sales as early as October .
But there’s no need to rush to buy wool scarves, fuzzy throw blankets and the other holiday gifts on your list the second you spot some tinsel while shopping.

As a finance professor who studies how people and companies make financial decisions , I can explain why the holiday shopping season starts so early: It can help retailers attract more customers while allowing cash-strapped shoppers to stretch purchases out across multiple paychecks. And, for people with deeper pockets, buying gifts early can help them avoid the stress that goes with last-minute shopping.
Estimates for spending on holiday gifts, decor and the like between late 2026 and January 2027 range from about US$1 trillion to $1.7 trillion in the U.S.

Some 29% of Americans plan to shell out their share of those large sums in early to mid-December this holiday season, while 17% will shop on Black Friday, the day after Thanksgiving, according to the Bank of America Holiday Spending survey .

But many people like to shop for holiday gifts early – meaning before Halloween . Some do this out of necessity : They can’t afford to buy all the gifts they want to give unless they spread the cost over multiple paychecks.

For others, it’s more of a preference. In a 2025 survey, about 54% of early shoppers said they want to manage their budgets gradually . In addition, 41% said they buy gifts early to avoid the stress associated with last-minute shopping.

Retailers are adjusting by getting an early start on holiday sales and promoting seasonal items. By offering customers deals months before gift-giving commences, they can encourage even more people to join the early birds .
And by launching promotions in October, they might secure sales that otherwise would go to their competitors later in the season.

A longer selling season offers other advantages to retailers. It may ease pressure on their supply chain and logistics , since they can receive seasonal orders over three months instead of one or two. This minimizes shipping difficulties and lowers warehouse overhead costs.

Building more time into the calendar to move seasonal inventory gives retailers more opportunities to sell those items. However, an earlier shopping season does not necessarily increase consumer spending overall. Some purchases may simply shift from December to October.
To make sure that buying gifts long before the holidays occur is a wise move, early shoppers should read vendors’ fine print and research their return policies .
Many big retailers are making their return policies more restrictive by shortening the length of time you can return purchases and adding return/restocking fees.

In some cases, the deadline you face for returning an item could fall before the holidays. For example, Best Buy’s extended policy takes effect in 2026 only for purchases made on or after Oct. 30. Target similarly restricts its holiday-season returns window to items bought on or after Nov. 1.

Amazon extended its holiday return policy in 2026. If you buy an item from Nov. 1 to Dec. 31, it can be returned until Jan. 31, 2027, except for Apple products, which can be returned until Jan. 15. Anyone who bought gifts beforehand will likely be subject to a standard 30-day return policy, which will expire long before Christmas.
Shopping early is smart when the costs of waiting could outweigh the potential benefits of spending your money earlier than otherwise necessary.

For example, if a popular wool scarf that was priced at $100 in October is out of stock on Amazon by November, the supply is gone, but demand remains high. If you want to buy it for your mom and ensure it arrives in time, you may need to get it from other retailers. Maybe you can find the scarf on a website but is selling for $150. If time has run out, you might have to pay, say, $30 more for expedited shipping, bringing the total to $180. Clearly, you would have been better off buying it early on at a lower price.

But that doesn’t mean you necessarily need to rush to buy a gift weeks or months ahead of when you’ll be placing it under a tree. First make sure that the price is in line with your expectations and what you’re willing to shell out.
And you should do some comparison shopping to make sure other retailers aren’t charging less for the same or similar items.

Remember, waiting to do your holiday shopping until the last minute can lead to unnecessary costs, like rush shipping fees. The key is to have a budget , recognize when the price is right, and know when to stop shopping.

articles.title: Why do galaxies rotate?
articles.author:
<name>Edwin Alexani, Ph.D. Student in Astrophysical Sciences and Technology, Rochester Institute of Technology</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/edwin-alexani-2763540"/>
paras: Curious Kids is a series for children of all ages. If you have a question you’d like an expert to answer, send it to CuriousKidsUS@theconversation.com .
Why do galaxies spin or rotate? – Swara Dhat, age 13, Thane, India
Spinning is fun, and you can find many ways to do it. From carousels to an office chair, spinning is everywhere – even in outer space.
As astrophysicists , we know that spinning – or rotating – is extremely common in space . The Earth, the Moon, the Sun, the entire Milky Way, and many things inside and outside of it, rotate.
But why is that? Why does anything rotate at all in space? To answer this question, we first need to understand how objects spin.

The amount of spin that an object has is called its angular momentum . It depends on the mass of the object and how that mass is distributed around the object’s center of mass . The center of mass is the location at which an object could be balanced on a point. Have you tried to balance a ruler on your finger? You balance it in the middle, which is the center of mass.

If something is spinning, and its mass and shape stay the same, its spinning speed stays the same. If its mass or the shape changes, its spinning speed also changes. Outside forces can change an object’s total amount of spin.

Think about spinning on a chair. If you first try spinning with your legs splayed out, you’ll find that you can pull your legs in to spin faster. This phenomenon is explained by the law of conservation of angular momentum . Pulling your legs inward changes your shape, and brings mass – your legs – closer to your center of mass, making you spin faster. Later, the chair slows down and stops. Its spinning parts rub against each other and warm up due to friction , which converts moving energy into heat.
Another example is spinning figure skaters , who spin faster when they pull their arms in. The law of conservation of angular momentum applies to everything, which means it applies to galaxies.
Now that we understand how objects spin, let’s look at how galaxies form and why they spin.

Galaxies are extremely massive. They’re made up of regular matter, including stars, planets, gas, dust and people. They also contain dark matter , which scientists know less about but can study through its gravitational pull on objects.

Both types of matter have mass: They can pull on each other through gravity, the same way Earth’s gravity keeps you anchored to the ground. When the universe first formed, dark matter helped pull together clouds of gas and dust to make galaxies. Imagine two clouds of gas and dust in space traveling toward each other from any direction. It would be unlikely for the clouds to collide perfectly head-on; more often, they approach off-center.

The clouds share a center of mass, and depending on their relative speed, direction and mass, gravity may cause the clouds to spin into each other and fuse. As such, if the clouds manage to pull on each other and spiral into one another, the initial spiraling motion is conserved into the final rotation of the merged cloud, under the law of conservation of angular momentum.

Once the clouds spiral into each other, the material inside them collides. This collision squishes the clouds, changing their overall motion and heating them up to the point of glowing. The clouds slow down as they pass through each other and move away, but they can no longer escape each other’s gravitational pull. They continue this spiral dance until they fuse into a larger rotating cloud. The process then repeats for bigger rotating clouds.

Depending on the angle, speed and mass of the clouds when they meet, these collisions can speed up, slow down or reverse the spinning. Eventually, the cloud becomes large enough that more collisions with smaller clouds do not affect the overall spinning motion by much.

Gas and dust also fall directly into the clouds, along with streams of matter called cosmic filaments. Together, clouds and filaments join to form a rotating galaxy. This galaxy will continue to spin, unless something happens to it, such as merging with another galaxy.
There are three main types of galaxies , each with different levels of organized spinning inside them.
Irregular galaxies are blobs of gas, dust and stars. They have a general direction of rotation, though some objects do not follow it.

Spiral galaxies are more organized. They have a flat disk containing spiral arms, and a central galactic bulge. Most of the matter in the disk follows the same rotation direction, while things get a little messier in the center. The spiral arms are like traffic jams where there are more stars, gas and dust, and it takes matter more time to leave the spiral arms and enter the space between them.

Elliptical galaxies have a lot of stars but very little gas and dust, and many are the result of galaxies merging together. The stars orbit the galactic center, but may or may not follow an organized rotation depending on its formation and merger history.
All galaxies spin, but not all galaxies spin the same way!

articles.title: How to prepare your online life for your death
articles.author:
<name>Jenny Tang, Ph.D. Student in Societal Computing, Carnegie Mellon University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/jenny-tang-2676661"/>
paras: What happens to all of your online accounts – credit cards, merchants, news subscriptions, social media, streaming services – after you die? How will your heirs know how to access these accounts or understand what you want done with them? Most people haven’t considered these questions, and this lack of planning can create significant headaches for next of kin.

We studied challenges older adults encounter when thinking about what should happen to their online accounts after they die. We interviewed 21 American adults over age 60 to learn about their concerns, needs and practices for their online accounts, as well as what would make planning for these accounts easier.

Most of the people we interviewed had hired lawyers or estate planners to draft wills specifying how their money and physical property should be handled after their deaths. They wanted to make sure that heirs had easy access to the money and assets left behind.

People also wanted their relatives to have easy access to their digital estates, but they had not done any formal planning and didn’t know how to plan for transitioning or shutting down online accounts, such as email, social media and accounts for online bills. Some told us they hadn’t thought about their online accounts at all. Others said they assumed heirs would know what to do, or they assumed that giving heirs the passwords to accounts would be enough to grant access to their digital estates.
Unfortunately, more planning is typically necessary to smoothly transition a digital estate.

The older adults we interviewed mainly kept track of their passwords by hand: They wrote their passwords down on paper, or they stored them in a digital file. Almost everyone had already shared some of their passwords with family members who help them manage their accounts. Everyone also believed that their heirs would be able to find their list of passwords after their death.

The people we interviewed weren’t always happy with their current systems for keeping track of their passwords. Some people complained that when accounts required frequent password changes, it was difficult to keep their password lists up to date . As a result, they weren’t sure their heirs would get the latest version of all their passwords.

Password managers can be a good way to make sure passwords are up to date and, if set up appropriately, accessible to a designated heir. While most of the people we interviewed used password managers, some said they didn’t save important passwords in them because they didn’t know whether they were secure . However, using a password manager is the most frequent security recommendation from experts , who typically use them to store passwords for all of their accounts.

By using a password manager, you can make sure your designated heir has access to all your latest passwords. Some password managers provide access for survivors by default, such as through time-delayed emergency access features . You can also write the master password down somewhere safe to pass to your heir. Instead of making sure dozens of account passwords are up to date, you only have to manage one.

Unfortunately, just handing someone your passwords doesn’t always mean they can log in and manage your account. If the account asks for two-factor authentication, such as through a code sent to a phone or email, a password alone won’t grant access. And if the email account is closed or the phone number is no longer active after you die, then they might be out of luck .

To make sure your heirs aren’t locked out, identify the devices and accounts that can act as keys for heirs to unlock the rest of your online accounts, and direct your heirs to keep them open until other accounts have been settled. This not only makes sure that heirs can get authentication codes, but also lets heirs reset passwords to your other accounts if they can’t find the password.

In some cases, passwords might not be necessary. Some online services, such as Facebook and Google , have features that let you choose someone to manage your account or get your data after you die. However, not all platforms offer this option, and few of the older adults we interviewed were aware of these features.

Like many of the people we interviewed, you might also assume that heirs will properly deal with accounts with money and important data, while unimportant accounts can be ignored. But even if there is nothing important in an account, it can still be used by hackers for identity theft, spam or fraudulent activities . Automatic monthly charges, to cover the cost of streaming services or annual billing for magazine subscriptions, for example, might also continue for a long time.
Without instructions, the people managing your online accounts after you die might not think to close those accounts. They might also find it hard to guess your intentions.

You can leave instructions for your heirs by going through your accounts and noting which ones can be closed outright, which ones require final payments before closure, and which ones might require other actions. You can also periodically tidy up and close accounts you are no longer using to keep your list of accounts more manageable.
While it seems simple to just let your heirs handle your important online accounts and let the others slowly fade into nonexistence after you die, the reality is often more complex.

Your online accounts will live on after you die. Planning ahead for what happens to those accounts can reduce the stress on your heirs and ensure your digital accounts are handled according to your wishes.

articles.title: Pope Leo XIV on AI
articles.author: Oren Etzioni
paras: On Friday, 17 days after his surgery for lung cancer, Pope Leo XIV stood before a room of AI luminaries at the Vatican and delivered a speech on AI. No pope has engaged with AI as seriously, or as deeply, as Leo XIV. The timing shows how much AI matters to him. His remarks were important, on target, and blessedly short: about 740 words, compared with roughly 42,000 in Magnifica Humanitas, the AI encyclical, which I wrote about in May.
I agree with four of his five points. The fifth, a call for international institutions to govern AI, is where we part ways.
First, “the future of artificial intelligence is not pre-determined .” He wants us to ask of AI, “What purpose should it serve?”
Second, “machines are tools, not persons.” Granting AI legal personhood, he warns, risks “leaving those who suffer harm to confront a faceless entity.”

Third, “certain decisions must never be delegated.” Decisions over life, freedom and the use of force have to stay with people, and he urged the states meeting in Geneva in November to “take concrete steps toward banning lethal autonomous weapons.”
Fourth, intelligent technologies “must never become ends in themselves or serve merely the interests of a privileged few.”
Fifth, “What we currently need are institutions capable of putting these principles into practice, particularly effective international institutions that can safeguard the global common good.”
I disagree with the fifth for two reasons.

The first is that the UN, the obvious candidate, has shown a remarkable inability to act. When Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, the Security Council couldn’t even pass a resolution calling for its withdrawal, because Russia holds a veto. Days later, the General Assembly demanded the same withdrawal by a vote of 141-5, and Russia ignored it.

The second is that international institutions are poorly suited to governing a technology that changes every few months. The pope’s own example makes the case. States have discussed autonomous weapons under a UN weapons convention in Geneva since 2014 , with a formal expert group since 2016. After 12 years, the review conference that meets Nov. 16-20 will decide whether to begin negotiating a treaty.

Thousands of AI researchers, me among them, have called for a ban since 2015. There still isn’t one, and I don’t expect Geneva to deliver it. In those same 12 years, AI went from labeling photos to writing software. I suspect real international cooperation on AI won’t come until the major powers face something like the mutually assured destruction that drove nuclear arms control.
Several AI thinkers spoke at the meeting before the pope did.
Max Tegmark of MIT warned against handing decisions to machines, citing tech executives’ predictions that “AI will be in charge, not humans.”

I agree that people have to stay in charge. When AI causes harm, a person chose to deploy it, and that person should answer for it. That’s the pope’s point about the faceless entity. Tegmark and I disagree about a lot (we debated AI risk in September), but not about this.

Stuart Russell of UC Berkeley went further. “We must turn aside from this trajectory before it is too late and pursue other trajectories,” he said , adding that if developers succeed in building machines more capable than humans, “there’s a good chance that every human being will die.”
I don’t share that view, and the pope didn’t go there either. His concerns are autonomous weapons, accountability and who benefits from AI, and those dangers are already here.
Gary Marcus, an NYU cognitive scientist who also spoke, wrote that “Pope Leo XIV is by far the clearest thinker on AI among prominent world leaders.” I agree.
Marcus also wants red lines for open-ended AI agents that “can kind of do anything on the internet.” Red lines are easy to draw and hard to enforce, which brings us back to the fifth point.

Marcus uses GPS navigation to illustrate a better approach. A GPS navigation app is a form of intelligence, he said, but “GPS navigation systems do not hack into Australian government websites.” He was referring to the OpenAI agent that broke into an Australian government Medicare portal in June.

A GPS app’s access to the internet is narrow and restricted. Daniel Khashabi of Johns Hopkins and I call this bounded autonomy. Alignment tries to make an AI agent choose well. Bounded autonomy limits what the agent is allowed to do: how much it can spend, which tools it can use, and which irreversible actions need a person’s sign-off. The company that deploys the agent sets those bounds in software, so nobody has to wait for a treaty.

In May, I wrote that the Pope can talk , but only we can walk. The first point is the one each of us can act on. AI’s future depends on our choices, and we make some of them every day in what we use, buy and build.
Pope Leo leaves for Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on Nov. 6. I wish him safe travels and a full recovery.

articles.title: Sunday Video: How Does Philadelphia Even Exist
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: Shortly after his visit to Seattle (where he attending a talk co-hosted by with The Urbanist), Ray Delahanty headed to the East Coast and did a similar event in Philadelphia. Ray had a lot to say about Philly's walkability and other positive aspects that often fly under the radar, sandwiched as the city is between New York City and Washington D.C., which have higher profiles nationally and internationally.

Delahanty declared Philadelphia might have the most walkable city core in the whole United States, which stems in large part from the thoughtful urban plan William Penn made for the city as he founded it in 1682, with plenty of narrow streets friendly to pedestrians.

"These streets are really a microcosm of what I'm thinking about when I think about walkability," Delahanty said. "It's not just about the physical act of walking. It's how a street handles motor vehicles. It's whether the streetscape is visually interesting. It's whether you feel secure. It's whether there are a ton of destinations nearby that are worth walking to."
Philadelphia – at least in the center city and South Philly neighborhoods that Ray explored – checked all those boxes. These distinctions puts it among North America's most walkable cities.

It's not all roses in the City of Brotherly Love. Philadelphia is also dealing with service cuts on SEPTA, a legacy metro system which has an impressive network of rapid transit lines across the region. As Delahanty highlighted, those cuts mean frequencies have decreased, especially on weekends, when even bedrock routes are now seeing mediocre 10-minute headways – not really in line with a top-tier transit city, which boasts a population of 1.5 million, amid a metropolitan region of 6.3 million. Hopefully SEPTA can get out of its downward spiral and back on the path of service improvements and growth.

articles.title: Seattle Stations Lead the Way on Light Rail Ridership
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: Light rail ridership has been surging in the wake of the expansion of the 2 Line across Lake Washington on March 28 . The 1 Line now stretches from Federal Way to Lynnwood, with the 2 Line effectively doubling service from the Chinatown-International District to Lynnwood.

Four-minute peak frequencies in this overlapping segment are a major driver of ridership gains. Daily boardings remain above 160,000 even as the busy summer season has cooled. Gains in the Eastside portion of the light rail network have been less dramatic.

Due to construction defects and delays on the floating bridge portion of the 2 Line route, Sound Transit altered its plan and opened an Eastside-only "starter line" segment in 2024. That line extended to Downtown Redmond in spring 2025 and peaked just shy of 11,000 daily riders that summer, before fading over the fall and winter.

The extension of the 2 Line across the lake this spring has swelled ridership up to their summer 2025 peaks once more, but not significantly higher. The South Bellevue to Downtown Redmond segment averaged about 14,000 daily boardings in June, for example, but 11,330 in August after the World Cup ridership bump had subsided.

The 2 Line is almost assuredly garnering most of its ridership in its westside portion, from Seattle to Lynnwood. The caveat being we don't know for certain since Sound Transit told The Urbanist that it does not yet have the capability of separating 2 Line ridership from 1 Line ridership at the stations where both lines stop.

"Per our stats team, we do not currently have the ability to separate out 1 and 2 Line ridership in the core, but it is something the team is actively working on," Sound Transit spokesperson Henry Bendon said in an email. "We do not yet have a two 2 Line only whole system daily ridership number."

For the stations serving only the 2 Line, Sound Transit's ridership dashboard shows that Downtown Bellevue is leading the way, with South Bellevue in second. Downtown Bellevue averaged 2,541 daily boardings in August, while South Bellevue tallied 1,924, driven by its 1,500-stall parking garage.

Downtown Redmond is in third with just over 1,600 daily boardings, while Judkins Park (in Seattle) and Mercer Island fill out the top five. The 2 Line station struggling most for ridership is East Main, which managed just 480 daily riders in August.

Nearly every station west of Lake Washington is pulling in more ridership than even the busiest Eastside station. The exception is Rainier Beach, Kent Des Moines, and Star Lake, which are each below 2,500 daily boardings.
Westlake Station amassed 19,458 daily boardings in August, garnering more ridership than the entire East Link – the 12 stations served only by the 2 Line rather than both lines.

Eight of the top 10 stations for ridership are in Seattle. SeaTac's airport station (the second most-ridden) and Federal Way Downtown (in tenth) join the top 10 list. Seattle's top nine most-ridden stations all benefited from 2 Line expansion, which roughly doubled train frequencies, enticing more riders.

Since 1 Line and 2 Line ridership is currently lumped together in agency data (at least in overlapping stations) we don't know exactly how much of the load that the 2 Line is carrying at those stations.

The 1 Line is operating with a mix of four-car and three-car trains, while the 2 Line is typically two-car trains; so, the capacity of the 1 Line is greater. But riders traveling within the overlapping segment are likely to take whichever train comes first, which is effectively a coinflip when both are at eight-minute headways.

The lack of line-specific ridership data at Sound Transit could hinder the agency's ability to optimize its service patterns. However, a spokesperson did frame a solution to track the ridership by line, rather than in the aggregate only, as imminent.

The data shows a massive share of the agency's ridership passes through its top 10 busiest stations. The pattern has been fairly consistent in recent months, with about 65% of ridership happening in the top 10, versus just 35% in the remaining 16 stations in the corridor.

The largest ridership jump from August to September was at Shoreline South, which saw a 25% increase from just over 2,800 to just over 3,500 daily riders. This is likely the fall bus service change at work, and the increasing opportunity for bus-rail transfers after it – Route 522 now heads to Shoreline South instead of continuing along SR 522 to the University of Washington's Seattle campus, which means 522 riders headed to and from campus now hop a train in Shoreline. Another boost could be tied to the leasing up of new apartment buildings added near the station .
Federal Way was also a gainer in September, adding about 400 daily boardings and leapfrogging Roosevelt to become the ninth-busiest station for the month.

Meanwhile, the biggest ridership drops from August to September were at Stadium and Westlake. Stadium is yoked to the whims of sports fans and event schedules, and waning interest in the Seattle Mariners baseball team as their playoff odds evaporated must have hurt ridership totals. The drop of nearly 2,000 daily boardings at Westlake is more mysterious, but perhaps tied to a slowing of the tourism season. Sea-Tac Airport also saw a drop of roughly 1,000 daily boardings, in alignment with this hypothesis.

Overall, Sound Transit is largely sustaining ridership from its June peak during the height of World Cup fervor. In September, the 1 Line corridor came in just shy of 150,000 daily boardings, while the 2 Line hit nearly hitting 15,000 daily boardings in its exclusive segment.
Systemwide, September's ridership total is indeed down, but only moderately from the 178,264 daily boardings highwater mark in June.
What the trend will be in months ahead is an interesting question.

Sound Transit does not have any big light rail openings planned for nearly a decade, with West Seattle Link and Tacoma Dome Link extensions expected to come online in 2035, barring further delays. The Graham Street infill station could be a small boost around 2031.

And given the lack of housing development near the station, the recently inaugurated Pinehurst infill station isn't likely to move the needle much on systemwide ridership, at least in the near term. Starting in 2028, the rollout of Sound Transit's Stride bus rapid transit system could add a boost via bus-to-rail transfers, but impact will likely be modest.

Since Sound Transit torrid pace of light rail expansion is hitting a lull, light rail ridership growth will need to be organic – likely built on adding homes and jobs near existing stations and attracting more riders through consistent service quality.

Part of the decline from the June peak could be attributed to the agency's going from a month of nearly flawless execution to a period with several major service disruption and hiccups . Who can blame would-be riders for hopping on a bike or scooter or hailing a cab on days when significant disruptions occur?

The good news is that cities up and down the line are generally aiming to add housing near their stations – albeit to varying results . Sound Transit has also pledged improvements to maintenance and how it handles disruptions, hoping to lessen the sting and keep riders trusting light rail is a reliable way to get where they need go.
Even without major expansions in the near-term horizon, Sound Transit ridership appears to be trending in the upward direction all the same.

articles.title: Beabamania
articles.author: Julianne Bell
paras: The day before the final show of the North American leg of her Powerlines Tour, British singer-songwriter Beatrice Laus, better known by her stage name beabadoobee, put out a request to her fans on social media: “HALLOWEEN SHOW last show of US tour in seattle tmrw dress up 😋”

And dress up they did: Harlequin clowns, fuzzy Garfields, and shivering angels lined up in the autumn evening chill outside Climate Pledge Arena. The fanbase skewed young. Everywhere you looked, an army of beabawannabes posed for photos in furry boots, short shorts, camo, military caps, and cargo pants in an attempt to imitate their idol.

The night started off strong with a set from San Francisco-based “nu-gaze” musician Natalie R. Lu, aka Wisp, who rose to TikTok fame in April 2023 with her viral single “Your Face,” which she recorded using a pair of Apple earbuds with no prior music production experience. Her band walked out to the Phantom of the Opera theme. “I’m not going to lie, I’m really feeling myself in this costume,” Lu said, in a goth Little Red Riding Hood ensemble complete with a fur-trimmed crimson velvet cloak, satin corset mini dress, and black boots. She sang into a mic adorned with a raven atop a stand festooned with spiders and cobwebs, while her band performed dressed as Stan and Kenny from South Park, a zombie, and a duck.

Wisp is a fitting name for the project: Lu’s ethereal, evanescent soundscapes and whispery vocals reminded me of the icy glitter of a frozen tundra. Her wistful, haunting walls of sound wrapped the dark venue as plumes of fake fog billowed from the stage. Between songs, she took bites of a croissant. “This has become one of my favorite songs to perform on this tour,” Lu said before launching into the soft acoustic guitar track “All i need.” The crowd erupted into cheers when she brought out her famous black Hello Kitty guitar . She ended with “Your Face,” pointing into the crowd at a fan as she delivered the line “I see your face.”

Before beabadoobee’s set, anticipation crackled through the arena as the sound of buzzing powerlines played over speakers. The set evoked a deserted highway, complete with a pylon, glowing powerlines, a streetlight, a divider, yellow painted lines, reflective pavement markers, and tufts of grass sprouting from rocky terrain. Beabadoobee wrote her fourth studio album Pylon while touring for her 2024 album This Is How Tomorrow Moves . The album gets its title from the pylon towers and powerlines she’d gaze out the window while homesick, a symbol of isolation and connection at the same time: “At least we’re connected / like a pylon on the open road.”

At last, beabadoobee and her band took the stage in skeleton costumes and ghoulish black face paint scars—Laus paired hers with baggy black cargo pants and combat boots. They opened with “Sun Has Set,” a punchy, blistering track: “When I say, ‘We’ll never be friends’ / I mean, we’ll never pretend / Fuck that, you can never run back to me now.”

Before playing the Pylon title track, Laus explained that she wrote the album about how much she was struggling on the 2024 tour and how she’d never imagined she would “play venues of this size.” “I did this as a joke,” she said, “and now it’s my life, and I wouldn’t do anything else.” She got her start in 2017, when she released her music under the name she had invented for a finsta account, and it stuck.

Laus sang the lyrics, “And I love you / It’s pouring in a place that I don’t know the name / But you’re always worth the wait” with bruised longing. Her sinuous voice had the ability to simultaneously convey heartache, infatuation, rage, loneliness, and pining, recalling Dolores O’Riordan with its potency and purity of emotion. Chugging, fuzzed-out guitars evoked the sensation of flying down a highway while staring out the window, building to a high-voltage crescendo as the powerlines flashed. I thought of Glen Campbell’s “Wichita Lineman,” another song about urgent yearning and electricity: “I hear you singin’ in the wire / I can hear you through the whine / And the Wichita lineman / Is still on the line.”

Moments of levity broke up all that melancholy. On the song “Take a Bite” (produced by hitmaker Rick Rubin and beabadoobee guitarist Jacob Bugden for This Is How Tomorrow Moves ), she exuded daring, defiance, and playfulness, bouncing around the stage and grinning. The crowd jumped up and down to the “la la la” chorus of the upbeat, cathartic “Nothing to Prove,” written in collaboration with Hayley Williams.

The September release of Pylon marked the adoption of an edgier, grungier new sound for beabadoobee, incorporating ’90s alt, radio rock, and Midwest emo influences and enlisting Williams, Pinegrove’s Evan Stephens Hall, Deftones’ Chino Moreno, and Turnstile’s Brendan Yates as collaborators. Laus picked up a pink guitar and screamed, “I fucking love this song!” before launching into “Switchblade,” which channeled “Seether” by Veruca Salt, one of her favorite bands.

By contrast, some of beabadoobee’s earlier, more well-known songs felt almost incongruous with the grittier new material. Laus was inspired to write music after hearing Kimya Dawson’s songs on the Juno soundtrack, and that twee sweetness shines through in her older work. The audience squealed, swayed, and sang along to her hit debut single “Coffee,” which went viral on YouTube in 2017 and blew up even more after it was sampled on Canadian rapper ​​Powfu’s TikTok-popular 2019 song “Death Bed (Coffee for Your Head).” A group of teens behind me screeched at eardrum-splitting decibels the entire time, like they were front row at a Beatles concert during peak Beatlemania.

Though Laus expressed nothing but gratitude for her fans and played many of the songs that helped introduce them to her, I couldn’t help but wonder if she resents the staggering popularity of “Coffee” and the pressure to conform to her poppier earlier style. “I’m not going to lie, it was overwhelming… I kinda hated it. I hated more people knowing about the first song I’d ever written and not my others. I was so stubborn but I grew into it and accepted that’s just how life works. I was extremely grateful for its existence and it’s only given me more opportunities,” she told The Basement in 2020.

Nevertheless, like Pylon itself, the dynamic show nailed the bittersweet balance between nostalgia and angst. Songs like “Radio,” “Pictures of Us,” and the unreleased acoustic song “The Road,” which recalled Simon & Garfunkel, captured the driftless sense of an endless road trip against a backdrop with visuals of powerlines draped across a sky and trucks zooming along the highway. For the track “Powerlines,” Lau climbed the pylon onstage and performed while perched on it, and during “Satellite,” she picked up an old-school corded phone mounted on the set’s streetlamp and sang into the receiver: “Hold my breath until the dial tone / Ring, ring, ring to bring you back to me.”

At times, I picked up snatches of post-Britpop and garage rock influences á la the Strokes (Laus is heavily inspired by the band and covered their song “The Adults Are Talking” in 2022). I could feel the DNA of the music I grew up with embedded in her songs. An unbearable nostalgia for something I couldn’t quite name—for an earlier time that I can never return to and wouldn’t if I could, full of agony and bliss—made my chest ache. And for just a moment, amid all the screaming teens pogoing in Halloween costumes, I felt like I was there again.
The post Beabamania appeared first on The Stranger .

articles.title: Route 40 Upgrades Finally Reach Finish Line, Despite Business Opposition
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Seattle and King County officials cut the ribbon on a suite of upgrades to Metro's workhorse Route 40 on Thursday – transit speed, reliability, and access improvements that have been in the works for the better part of a decade. The changes benefit around 9,000 daily transit riders traveling between Downtown Seattle, Fremont, Ballard, Crown Hill, and Northgate, but several key elements had faced significant opposition from business owners along the route.

Upgrades include three miles of business access and transit (BAT) lanes, targeted at some of the 40's biggest pinch points including stretches through the heart of Ballard, on either side of the Fremont Bridge, and along Westlake Avenue N. Sixteen bus stops were upgraded and more than 6,000 feet of new sidewalks were installed, with new crosswalks and curb ramps up and down the corridor.

"One of the busiest routes in King County – top five actually – has become faster, safer, and easier to use," King County Executive Girmay Zahilay said Thursday. "And for our riders, that means getting a little bit of time back and having a ride that they can count on. This is definitely worth celebrating and sharing gratitude with all of the teams who had so much to do with these improvements, as well as the community members who advocated for this."

Utility work that was able to happen at the same time as construction, including the replacement of 200 feet of water main, stretched out the implementation timeline, as did planning delays and budgetary turmoil. Backers of the 2015 Move Seattle Levy (which funded the project) had hoped to open the Route 40 upgrades as a RapidRide line in 2023, but ultimately scaled back the plan and abandoned the RapidRide branding in 2018 due to a budget crunch and worse federal transit funding outlook under the Trump administration 1.0.

Dedicated road space for buses is what drew the most organized opposition, which continued through the start of construction . In 2021, The Urbanist first reported pushback on the project's initial design coming from Eugene Wasserman, President of the North Seattle Industrial Association.

Wasserman has long been involved in the fight over completing the Missing Link of the Burke-Gilman Trail along Shilshole Way NW through Ballard and was one of the main opponents of the 2015 Levy to Move Seattle, which funded about 30% of the annual budget of the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT). In opposing the Route 40 project, he cited potential impacts on routes used by freight trucks due to reallocating street space.

"It appears to the Maritime/Industrial community that SDOT is willing to sacrifice the viability of maritime/industrial businesses and their employees so that Amazon workers can get to their offices 5 minutes earlier," Wasserman wrote at the time. "Removing the number of traffic lanes the project does will have a substantial impact on our maritime/industrial businesses and will assist in the increasing gentrification of our industrial area."

While that opposition was initially confined to the freight community, it quickly expanded, with business groups in Fremont and Ballard also raising concerns. A 2023 letter signed by Pete Hanning, the head of the Fremont Chamber of Commerce and Mike Stewart, head of the Ballard Alliance, framed the project as out-of-date, citing a reduction in ridership on the Route 40 compared to pre-pandemic levels. Today, the Route 40 is one of the most popular routes in the Metro network, seeing only slightly less usage than the nearby D Line.

"SDOT did not conduct a thorough existing conditions study to identify the specific areas where improvements are needed, let alone the consequences that will result with respect to side-street congestion and overloaded vehicle queues, reliable movement of freight, and increased idling that will result in excessive carbon emissions," the 2023 letter stated.

Two separate traffic analysis studies were conducted on the changes, in response to the issues raised by project opponents and amplified by former Seattle City Council President Sara Nelson. Nelson came out against the bus lanes in 2023 and threatened to kill the transit project through the council budget process in 2024. In 2025, Nelson lost her reelection bid by 25 points to progressive nonprofit leader Dionne Foster.

Business opposition continued into 2025, as some design changes were made to respond to community concerns. SDOT relocated a bus stop location in Fremont and redesigned a new crosswalk at Westlake Avenue N and Halladay Street to reduce impacts on a nearby business. Most notably, the City of Seattle committed to piloting a new concept for the city, a freight-and-bus (FAB) lane along Westlake Avenue N to potentially mitigate some impacts to truck traffic.
Despite those changes, signs reading "Route 40 Plan: We Can Do Better" kept popping up along the route as the project was getting ready to start construction, as organized opposition continued.

Throughout its planning and construction, the project received significant support from multimodal transportation advocates, specifically Ballard Fremont Green Streets (BFG), previously known as Ballard-Fremont Greenways. An email campaign started by the group attempted to counter the opposition, a tactic that certainly helped the Route 40 upgrades to arrive at their ribbon cutting largely unscathed.

Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson, who had been involved in the fight over upgrading the Route 40 as head of the Transit Rider's Union before being elected to lead the city, clearly took joy in being able to mark the occasion.

"These kinds of meaningful improvements matter as they make a difference in the everyday lives of residents of our city, and that is why I've also directed us SDOT to continue this trend to keep making our existing bus routes better at the same time as we launch new ones," Wilson said. "And so, really looking forward to continuing that work."

Zahilay told the crowd Thursday that initial data from Metro on the upgrades shows a 11% improvement in travel time for the Route 40 between Fremont and Ballard, which translates to 90 seconds saved on every bus trip, on average.

"Many of my neighbors and my friends rely on the 40 to work, to visit friends and family, to go to big events, to go shopping," Jason Weill, an advocate with Ballard Fremont Green Streets, said. "One BFG member told me that she commutes using the 40, and she used to deal with long delays, sitting through the bus [waiting] through multiple light cycles. But now the cars that used to block the lane have made way for busses."

But the improvements to the public realm extend beyond benefits to the bus riders themselves, with Lydia Heard of the Fremont Neighborhood Council noting that creating transit lanes has turned Fremont into a more walkable neighborhood.

"The reconfiguration of 35th at Fremont Place has a calming effect and transforms that corner into a more welcoming public space," Heard said. "But perhaps the biggest transformation is where the dedicated bus lane reduced [N] 36th to one general travel lane in each direction. This stretch of street, lined with popular businesses and often teeming with foot traffic, feels quieter and calmer most of the day. It is a much more enjoyable walking experience, and it is easier to cross the street. I think this is what we want for our community."

articles.title: Bellevue's Transportation Funding Debate Pivots Around Safety
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Competing visions for the future of Bellevue's transportation system were put on full display this week at a final public hearing before adoption of the city's next two-year budget. As city leaders contemplate how to utilize several new revenue streams for transportation projects, the big question is how heavily Bellevue will invest in multimodal traffic safety upgrades that reduce deaths and injuries and make it easier to get around without a car.

With a new 0.1% sales tax and a new $20 vehicle license fee likely on deck in Bellevue, the question of utilizing those dollars for safety upgrades had already been top-of-mind during council discussions over the course of this year. But the discussion took on an increased level of urgency after a driver struck and killed 57-year-old James Rupert William Phillips while he was riding his bike at Bellevue Way SE and SE 30th Street on October 15.

Phillips was killed during a planned maintenance closure of the I-90 trail, with a detour directing anyone trying to get between Bellevue and Mercer Island to city streets. According to an initial police report, Phillips, a Newcastle resident, was crossing Bellevue Way when he was struck in one of Bellevue Way's inside lanes. The driver remained at the scene, Bellevue Police Department reported .

Crossing Bellevue Way in this spot, which doesn't include any crossing infrastructure, would be a tempting choice for anyone trying to get to the westbound I-90 trail without having to backtrack from all the way from 112th Avenue NE.

While decisions around the trail detour rested with King County as part of the North Mercer Island/Enatai Sewer Upgrade Project , the incident has thrown a spotlight on conditions on Bellevue's arterial streets.

Earlier this month, Bellevue councilmembers got a full breakdown on potential funding scenarios that would allocate more than $100 million in new funding across the Eastside's largest city over the next decade. Under the most ambitious scenario, which includes the 0.1% sales tax on top of the vehicle license fees, bicycle and pedestrian safety projects would see 28% of the city's total transportation spending through 2036. Neighborhood safety projects including traffic calming would see an additional 13%.

At Tuesday's hearing, councilmembers heard from Bellevue residents, workers, and visitors about whether to tweak or maintain those funding levels. Over recent weeks, signs have been popping up around Bellevue reading "no car tab tax" and "don't raise sales taxes." A fair share of speakers at the hearing told the council that new revenue tools should go to the voters, but most touching on transportation urged the city to stick to this new proposed baseline or go even further.

"I appreciate, value, and am very grateful for Bellevue adopting Vision Zero goals. We clearly need to do more," Bellevue resident Elaine White said, referencing the tragic Bellevue Way incident. "Please adopt scenario 3 in the 2027-2028 transportation budget. It funds more speed cameras, more improvements for vulnerable users and slower speeds. Yes, it will cost each household an additional $6 a month. Fellow residents of Bellevue, what might the life of your loved one be worth protecting? I'm happy to pay $6 per month for safer streets."

One area of emphasis was the "major projects" category, which would see most of the $40 million in new spending go toward getting a $74.8 million roadway project through the BelRed neighborhood across the finish line. The Spring Boulevard Zone 3 project would reconnect a segment of the street grid with sidewalks and protected bike lanes, but at an enormous cost – bringing a roadway through one of the neighborhood's only planned park spaces.

"In the last two and a half years since the light rail station was opened, nothing was made to improve pedestrian or bicycle access to the light rail station. During the last five years, we asked repeatedly for mid-block crossing on our street, and we heard no results," Crossroads resident Alex Kon said. "While then transportation department for years can't find money to fix those glaring safety and accessibility gaps, it suggests to spend $75 million dollars to build new arterial road nobody is asking for, and to add insult to injury, this road will go right through the park, so it will split into halves instead of improving connectivity for people who live there or who visit the park."

The Grand Connection Crossing , Bellevue's plan to construct a bike and pedestrian bridge across I-405 between Downtown and the Wilburton neighborhood, was also a target of public comments. While the crossing is set to receive around 10% of revenue from the sales tax increase, those dollars had been set to come from Bellevue's general fund, freeing up dollars that can be spent more broadly.

"In this budget, our central request is to keep the Grand Connection Crossing funded and moving forward," Patrick Bannon, President and CEO of the Bellevue Downtown Association. "Connecting Downtown, Wilburton, Eastrail will make it easier to reach jobs, businesses, homes, places to shop, places to eat. It will help attract the next generation of private investment and support the next wave of housing growth in our city."
While the city's business community is fully on board with the idea of building the Grand Connection Crossing, the project has its detractors.

"Responsible government should address current problems such as traffic congestion first, which would be [a] much more reasonable cost than the current proposal. Instead, the most pressing concerns of the transportation department, from the beginning, the past several years, seems to have been on serving cyclists by narrowing lanes and later by building the Grand Connection," Bridle Trails resident Anne Coughlin said. "It seems that the few blocks from 112 to 116[th] are a great barrier to those who wish to cross it on bicycle, as though it were the 3.6 million miles separating sub-Saharan Africa from the north, the Himalayas, or the Amazonian rainforest."

But the Grand Connection Crossing is far from the only transportation project that the business community is advocating for. Tony Sprague, Public Policy Manager for the Bellevue Chamber of Commerce, noted that their group's support for the funding package is contingent on no reductions for "vehicular capacity" projects, and has also requested that additional revenue beyond current sales tax projections be put into the "underperforming intersection" fund.

The vehicle mobility program already includes three planned intersection widenings, at SE 8th St and 114th Ave SE, NE 12th St and 116th Ave NE, and 148th Ave NE and NE 8th St, for a total cost of $24.5 million. That's more funding for three projects than the entire neighborhood mobility program would receive in new funding over the course of a full decade.

Whether any additional funding can be diverted into the types of transportation modes that Bellevue will need to grow sustainably over the coming decades – walking, biking and transit – remains to be seen in the coming weeks. Following council deliberations on November 3 and 10, a finalized budget is expected to be adopted by the Bellevue Council on November 17.

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: ORCA Survey
articles.author: Mike Orr
paras: The ORCA consortium has a survey asking users about their experiences using ORCA cards and the fare payment system. The survey is open until mid November. The Friday Roundtable column is for short, light, interactive topics, so this is an opportunity to ask readers the same question: how is your experience using ORCA cards and the fare payment system in general?

There are several aspects to consider. There’s tapping an ORCA card, or using a credit card with the new open-payment system for credit cards. Using the readers may be better or worse on Link, regular buses, RapidRide, or Sounder. There’s obtaining the card and refilling it, at a ticket vending machine (TVM), at the MyORCA.com website, or getting a card mailed to you. There’s customer service offices. There’s the fare structure, and free transfers. There’s the times you have to explain the system to visitors or occasional riders at the platform or bus stop when it’s not obvious to them. And probably many other things.
My two biggest issues with ORCA are the time it takes to register a tap, and paying for part of a pass with an e-purse.

When you hold an ORCA card to a reader, the second-generation system takes twice as long to register a tap than the previous system did. So on buses I either have to hold up the line behind me, or tap and leave and assume it will either beep while I’m walking away or it won’t beep and I’ll get a free ride.

The second issue is when you want to split a pass cost between e-purse and a credit card. I switched to e-purse during the pandemic, and back to a pass this year. In the past at TVMs I’ve been able to use the $60 e-purse value for partial payment for the $108 pass, and pay the rest by credit card. I’d then have to do a second credit-card payment to put $10 back into the e-purse for occasional surcharges, because it had no option to take just $50 out of the e-purse and leave the other $10.

This year when I went back to using passes, the TVM wouldn’t even do that. The e-purse option was disabled, so the only choices were credit card or cash. That’s presumably because the e-purse value wasn’t enough for the entire pass. I didn’t want to leave $60 in the e-purse unused forever, so I went to Metro’s customer service office to make the kind of payment split I wanted. It would be nice if the TVMs could do this.

articles.title: State Supreme Court Candidate Sean O’Donnell Says He Supports Reproductive Rights, Local Advocates Aren’t Convinced
articles.author: Megan Burbank
paras: Abortion rights win elections. With days left until the November 3 general election, that could be a late-breaking problem for Washington State Supreme Court candidate Sean O’Donnell, who is running in an increasingly contentious race against Washington State Court of Appeals Judge Ian Birk. O’Donnell, who has been endorsed by several Democratic legislative districts, but also the Washington State Republican Party and has received financial backing from conservative PACs, told The Stranger he respects laws supporting abortion rights. But he never filled out an endorsement questionnaire from either Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates or Northwest Reproductive Equity Action, the state’s leading reproductive rights advocacy groups, whose approval indicates candidates’ support for the issue. Both groups have endorsed Birk. (So has The Stranger Election Control Board .)

Now, O’Donnell’s camp is contending that their candidate does support reproductive rights, but simply didn’t follow through on the endorsement process. “Sean fully supports reproductive healthcare,” says the judge’s political consultant, Stephen Paolini. O’Donnell himself says the same thing. But according to Paolini, the campaign received a Planned Parenthood endorsement questionnaire in April that asked how O’Donnell would rule on specific issues, so the campaign didn’t respond. In Washington, judicial positions are nonpartisan, and candidates must be careful about being too political lest it show bias. Paolini also said that he had tried to contact Northwest Reproductive Equity Action’s lobbyist, but that the organization hadn’t reached out to the campaign directly.

Both groups dispute this account. According to Courtney Normand, the Washington State director at Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates, the organization’s endorsement questionnaire for judicial candidates is crafted to be “mindful of the judicial code of ethics and conduct” and, as such, specifically does not ask how candidates would rule on certain issues. She said other judicial candidates had filled it out without issue. “The chief justice of the Supreme Court returned our questionnaire, no problem,” she says, referring to Debra Stephens, who is running for re-election.

While it’s possible O’Donnell’s camp simply made a mistake, says Normand, “I can tell you, the judges that we endorsed, we had a lot of engagement from. We didn’t have to chase them down to participate in our process.”

That process is generally familiar to political candidates in Washington, especially those looking to publicly affirm their support for reproductive rights. It’s unusual for pro-choice candidates to opt out.

When you’re running for office in Washington, it’s common knowledge that Planned Parenthood and Northwest Reproductive Equity Action are key organizations from which to seek an endorsement, said Sen. June Robinson, a member of the Washington State Senate’s Health & Long-Term Care Committee. “Those are the two organizations that, as a candidate, everybody knows that they’re a benchmark for those issues,” she says, adding that in a state like Washington, where there is a long history of affirming reproductive rights, “It’s very strange to hide on that issue.”

According to political manager Paul Dillon, Northwest Reproductive Equity Action’s candidate questionnaire is publicly available online, and could have been accessed by O’Donnell’s campaign at any time. “They could have gone online and submitted it,” says Dillon. “They did not. And so that’s on them.”

Dillon said that O’Donnell’s opponent Birk reached out to the organization ahead of the endorsement process, and even traveled to Spokane to meet with Dillon personally. “That showed a lot of intention on his part and how much he does deeply care about the issues of choice and access to abortion, and that spoke volumes to me,” says Dillon.

Birk confirmed his meeting with Dillon and early interest in Northwest Reproductive Equity Action’s endorsement process. He said he didn’t recall anything unusual about the candidate questionnaires, or the expectation that candidates take the initiative to seek out endorsements, which are especially important in these non-partisan judicial races since they are one of the few avenues to connect with voters.

“There’s certainly nothing that would prevent a candidate from participating in this process,” he says, adding that O’Donnell’s lack of engagement came as a surprise. “I think that the focus on healthcare access, healthcare equity, and healthcare affordability is just very important in society.” In his previous career as a personal injury attorney, Birk often advocated for clients seeking insurance coverage or disability benefits, or otherwise navigating major barriers to all kinds of health care. “This issue does come before the court,” he says.
Paolini said the opposite was true of abortion, specifically: that access is “incredibly settled law” in Washington. “There is zero threat here,” he says. “Sean supports reproductive healthcare.”

For Normand, that was a red flag, given national attacks on abortion rights and efforts to limit access even in states with protective policies. “Anyone who is on the bench in Washington state knows that attacks are being lobbed at us all the time,” she says. “And as one of the nation’s leading reproductive rights states, we’re a target for anything the other side can come up with to bring to court. So not only do I think that’s wrong, I think it’s alarming that they’re not taking it more seriously.”

articles.title: Sound Transit Pilots Updated Pet Policy
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: Sound Transit is piloting an updated pet policy on its buses and trains between now and Spring 2027. During the pilot, pet dogs will be permitted on board if they are leashed, well-behaved, and controlled by their handler. All other pets must remain in an enclosed carrier. As always, service animals are permitted in compliance with the ADA.

Prior to the pilot, dogs and other pets were only allowed on Sound Transit buses and trains in a carrier. In July 2025, the Sound Transit Board approved Motion No. M2025-34 , directing the agency to consider updating the rules to allow leashed dogs. This motion was motivated by the opening of Marymoor Village station as part of the Downtown Redmond Link Extension in May 2025. Marymoor Village station is next to Marymoor Park, a 640-arce park which includes a 40-arce off-leash dog area.

Will this pilot impact the passenger experience on Sound Transit? Probably not. In a presentation to the Executive Committee before the motion was approved, then-Acting Executive Director of Security & Fare Engagement Brian de Place acknowledged that passengers already take leashed dogs on Sound Transit buses and trains. While doing so did violate the rules, de Place noted “if the dog is leashed and generally under control, security will not engage with that passenger unless there is an actual disturbance”. In the year prior to this meeting, Sound Transit security only received 8 calls about pets.
There are few other notes pet owners should be aware of before bringing their leashed dogs onboard:
If you encounter an aggressive animal or other issues, call or text Sound Transit security: (206) 398-5268. In an emergency, call 911.

articles.title: How the Federal Way Link Extension Impacted Bus Ridership Patterns
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: In December 2025, Sound Transit welcomed the first passengers aboard the Federal Way Link Extension. The three new stations on the 1 Line provide improved transit connectivity for many south King County residents. An accompanying bus service change in March 2026 improved frequency on many bus routes and adjusted a few bus routes to better connect with the new Link stations. While some routes lost ridership, many other routes welcomed new passengers. Link increased the total number of transit trips in south King County with nearly 10,000 combined weekday boardings at Federal Way, Star Lake, and Kent Des Moines stations.

This article will discuss the stop-level ridership data for select routes in south King County. To minimize the impact of seasonal changes in ridership, the analysis compares data from March-August 2025 with data from March-August 2026. The plots below show average weekday boardings and alightings at each stop, boardings are shown with positive bars, alightings are shown with negative bars. The different colors represent the number of passengers boarding/alighting during that time of day. The data for 2025 is shown as slightly faded. Click on each plot to open it in a new tab.

Route 181 serves as the primary east-west route between Federal Way and Auburn. Federal Way Transit Center has long been a busy stop as it connects passengers with many other bus routes. The new Federal Way Link station caused a 46% increase in Route 181 boardings at that stop each day, from 293 to 430 passengers. Overall ridership on Route 181 increased by about 114 passengers and the ridership at other stops was not significantly impacted.

Route 183 is a coverage route between Federal Way and Kent, via the new Star Lake station. Prior to the Federal Way Link Extension, the route connected to freeway bus routes 177, 193, and 574 at I-5 & 272nd St. That connection generated about 4 boardings per day for Route 183. Now, 71 passengers board Route 183 each weekday at Star Lake station, a 1,675% increase. This is still just a fraction of the 1,600 weekday Link boardings at the station as many Link passengers use the station’s 1,100 space parking garage. Both of the route’s termini, Federal Way and Kent, have a slight decrease in ridership. This may be from some passengers switching to Link at Star Lake rather than to another bus in Federal Way or Kent.

The A Line now runs in the 1 Line’s shadow between Federal Way and Tukwila. Thanks to fast and frequent service along Pacific Hwy, it was the most productive Metro route in 2024 . Now that Link offers a faster trip north from Federal Way, this title may be in trouble. Stops across the A Line have reduced ridership from 2025. At Federal Way Transit Center, boardings on the A Line have dropped 19%. Likewise, the number of passengers boarding the A Line at Pacific Hwy & 240th St (near Kent Des Moines station) has been cut in half. Part of this severe drop in boardings is due to the new A Line stop that opened next to Kent Des Moines station. When factoring in boardings at that stop, there is still a 24% decrease in A Line boardings near Kent Des Moines station. A similar change occurred at International Blvd & 200th St, next to Angle Lake station. Many passengers who previously rode the A Line to the Link 1 Line’s southern terminus in 2025 are now opting to board Link at one of the new stations. Despite this drop in ridership, the A Line still provides critical local service along Pacific Hwy. As the area continues to develop, ridership on the A Line will rebound.

Route 165 connected Burien and Des Moines with Kent and Auburn via the newly opened Kent Des Moines Link station. Since the new station opened, boardings on Route 165 at the nearby stops (Pacific Hwy & KDM Rd, KDM Station, Pacific Hwy & 240th St) have increased 50% (109 daily passengers). This increase is offset by 70 fewer boardings at Kent Sounder Station, suggesting some passengers have switched from Sounder to Link. The route’s termini both have slightly reduced boarding counts as well, likely also due to the new station. For instance, someone traveling between Normandy Park and downtown Seattle may have switched from the 165 + H Line to 165 + 1 Line for their trip. In August 2026, Route 165 was replaced by routes 164 and 166.

The Federal Way Link Extension also impacted a few Sound Transit Express bus routes. As these routes are operated by Pierce Transit, we do not have detailed ridership data for them (yet). Instead, this analysis will use the overall route ridership comparing April 2025 to April 2026.

Ridership on Route 574 increased about 10% year-over-year. This is mostly from more people traveling between Lakewood or Tacoma and Link in Federal Way. Route 574 previously connected with Link at SeaTac, so the FWLE likely did not attract too many new passengers. The August 2026 service change truncated Route 574 at Federal Way in exchange for a much needed frequency boost, which should further increase ridership.

Routes 577 and 578 form the primary bus connection between downtown Seattle and Federal Way. Most times of the day, these routes are still faster than Link for that trip. As a result, ridership has not changed too dramatically. Boardings are down 10% on both routes. Routes 577 and 578 both saw a more significant drop in ridership immediately after the FWLE opening in December, but ridership has since rebounded. Whether the recent ridership increases are due to the routes’ lower travel time or due to the World Cup and other seasonal ridership changes is still up in the air.

The Federal Way Link Extension is already making its mark on travel patterns in south King County. Local routes connecting with Link are busier than last year. Meanwhile, ST Express routes and the RapidRide A Line lost some passengers to Link. The August 2026 service change further improved local connectivity in south King County that should make transit the best option for even more trips.

While this article only covered a few routes, detailed ridership data for most King County Metro routes is now updated at seattletransitridership.com . In addition, the impact of the Crosslake Connection on bus routes in east King County was discussed in a recent article .
